articles.title: CONEXPO-CON/AGG 2026 recap

paras.en: CONEXPO-CON/AGG 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada, reaffirmed its position as the largest construction trade show in North America, drawing more than 140,000 construction professionals from 128 countries across the globe. For Carlisle Brake & Friction, a CentroMotion brand, the week was an incredible opportunity to showcase innovation, strengthen partnerships and gain valuable insights into the future of the construction, mining and aggregate industries. Throughout the busy week, attendees had the chance to speak with our experts and watch live demonstrations of our brake systems, along with our advanced brake and transmission friction solutions for the construction industry.

paras.en: CONEXPO-CON/AGG is more than a trade show, it’s a barometer for where the industry is headed. Top trends included integrating autonomous equipment, advanced digital tools and sustainable technologies. The exhibition footprint spanned more than 3 million square feet with greater than 2,000 exhibitors, and attendees covered miles of exhibits sprawled across indoor and outdoor spaces.

At the show, Carlisle Brake & Friction highlighted its advanced brake systems and friction technologies designed to withstand extreme duty cycles and demanding off‑highway applications. Attendees experienced firsthand the performance, quality, and engineering expertise that define the CarlisleCBF brand. The CentroMotion booth was a hub of activity, and the team welcomed OEM leaders and aftermarket specialists. These interactions went beyond showcasing our products, they enhanced relationships and increased our team’s understanding of the industry’s evolving needs. Check out this video https://youtu.be/C_IaFtvWBY8 for more detail about our booth and featured products serving the market.

paras.en: The show floor was packed with the latest advancements across construction, aggregate, concrete and lifting. Attendees explored:
• New and upgraded equipment and machinery in action
• Advances in automation, electrification and equipment intelligence
• Digital tools focused on productivity, fleet management and jobsite visibility
• Solutions designed to improve safety, efficiency and sustainability
Hands on demos and a live equipment showcase gave attendees the opportunity to see innovations in action and understand how they can be applied on real jobsites.
Technology continued to be a major focus at CONEXPO-CON/AGG 2026. Exhibitors and education sessions highlighted these key updates as transformational in construction operations:
• Digital workflows and jobsite visibility
• Sustainability and emissions reduction
• Workforce challenges and talent development
Together, these topics reflected an industry adapting to change while looking toward long term growth.
Looking ahead: The future of construction

CONEXPO-CON/AGG shines a bold spotlight on the companies and innovations redefining what’s next in the construction, mining and aggregate industries. Our team’s conversations and key learnings will help shape our strategies for the coming year, and we’re committed to driving progress!

articles.title: New Facility Brings Off-Highway Wet Friction Production to India

paras.en: New Facility Brings Off-Highway Wet Friction Production to India

Carlisle Brake & Friction has broken ground to expand its Chennai, India manufacturing operations in one of the world’s fastest-growing industrial regions. Having produced mechatronic products in the region for more than 15 years, Carlisle CBF will relocate to add production at a larger site for off-highway paper wet friction discs and steel separator plates. The new facility is scheduled to open in 2027.

The move to expanded space is designed to accommodate manufacturing capabilities needed to serve the growing demand across the agriculture, construction and especially mining industries in India and Southeast Asia. Local production will improve supply chain responsiveness while supporting original equipment and aftermarket requirements in cost-sensitive markets.

Carlisle Brake & Friction is establishing a state-of-the-art wet friction manufacturing facility on par with proven global manufacturing processes in the new Chennai plant, to build a more resilient regional platform. This expansion strengthens our ability to deliver durable wet friction products that help keep critical off-highway equipment productive.

articles.title: Vermont Insurance Study Calls for Changes to Labor Rate, Appraisal and Aftermarket Parts Rules
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: A comprehensive study by the Vermont Department of Financial Regulation (DFR) has identified shortcomings in how auto insurers determine collision repair labor rates, handle appraisals and disclose the use of aftermarket parts, prompting recommendations for changes to the state’s insurance claims regulations.

The 52-page report, dated Dec. 31, 2025, was prepared in response to Act No. 32 of 2023, which directed the department to examine whether auto insurers’ labor rates, parts practices and other business procedures are fair and reasonable.

Among its most significant findings, DFR concluded that insurers’ methods for establishing prevailing labor rates are frequently inconsistent, inadequately documented or based on information that may not accurately represent the repair marketplace.
The department recommends amending Vermont Insurance Regulation I-79-2 to establish clearer standards for determining labor rates, resolving payment disputes and protecting consumers.
The report also addresses DRPs, total loss valuations, virtual appraisals, repair estimating practices and the potential effects of regulatory changes on insurance premiums.

Labor rates emerged as a central issue in the study, with collision repairers expressing concerns that insurer reimbursement has failed to keep pace with operating expenses, technician wages and increasingly complex vehicle repairs.

According to the department’s survey of Vermont collision repair facilities, shops reported hourly body labor rates ranging from $60 to $84, with an average of $67. The average reported rate had increased 26% since 2020.

By comparison, insurer data showed an unweighted mean reimbursement rate of $60.50 in 2024, up from $44.33 in 2010. The report cautioned that this measure combines different labor categories and is only a rough indicator of average costs, rather than a direct comparison with shops’ average body labor rate.
The department surveyed 25 collision repair facilities, representing approximately 17% of the 147 shops it identified. It also collected information from 20 insurance companies or insurance groups.

Eleven of the 20 insurer respondents reported using aggregated information from CCC ONE and/or NuGenIT to determine prevailing labor rates. Other insurers relied on geographic data, surveys, proprietary estimating tools or their own appraisal histories.
Although insurers maintained that their methods reflected prevailing marketplace rates, DFR found problems when it examined how those methods were applied.
The report states that insurer procedures for determining labor rates are often inconsistent, may fail to produce representative market rates and are not always clearly documented.

It also found that some insurers relied on information derived from direct repair agreements or previously negotiated insurance settlements to establish prevailing rates. Such information may reflect amounts insurers have already agreed to pay rather than independently established market prices.

Additionally, the department identified instances in which insurers appeared to compensate for labor rate differences through separate estimate or supplement line items, potentially obscuring the actual labor rate used to settle a claim.
DFR acknowledged that collision repair businesses also bear responsibility for understanding their costs and establishing defensible rates.
The department recommended creating objective standards for insurers to identify average market labor rates, along with documentation requirements and procedures for handling disagreements.
Rather than recommending a statewide minimum reimbursement rate, DFR favored regulatory changes designed to make labor rate determinations more transparent and consistent.
Virtual Appraisals and Supplements Raise Concerns
The department also identified problems associated with insurers’ growing reliance on photo-based estimating and virtual appraisals.
According to the shop survey, respondents reported that supplemental estimates were required on an average of 95% of repairs. Ten shops said they needed supplements on every repair.
Shops reported an average repair delay of 7.32 days associated with the supplement process.
The department cautioned that insurer-provided data did not show the same magnitude of increase in supplements reported by repair facilities.

Nevertheless, DFR found that virtual adjusting can result in incomplete initial estimates, additional administrative work for repairers and delays while shops await approval to order parts or proceed with repairs.

The study also found that 72% of responding shops said insurers would not send an appraiser when requested by the repair facility, while 76% said insurers would not send one at the customer’s request.

DFR recommends amending its regulations to establish deadlines for responding to and paying supplements. It also recommends formalizing previous guidance requiring in-person inspections when consumers request them, ensuring access to qualified Vermont-licensed appraisers and prohibiting insurers from discouraging those requests.
The department further recommended requiring insurers to document and justify significant deviations from estimating software guidance.
Aftermarket Parts Disclosures Recommended

The study also examined the use of aftermarket and recycled parts, including potential cost savings, quality concerns and the additional labor sometimes required to make replacement components fit properly.
DFR acknowledged that aftermarket parts can reduce repair costs and may be easier to obtain than OEM components.

However, the report found that fit and modification problems can arise and that most responding repair facilities said they were not reimbursed for additional labor and paint materials associated with modifying insurer-required aftermarket parts.
The department recommends adopting disclosure requirements consistent with the National Association of Insurance Commissioners’ model regulation.
It also plans to explore requiring insurers to identify aftermarket parts used in calculating claims settlements.

DFR did not recommend requiring OEM parts for vehicles within a specified age range. If lawmakers pursue such a requirement, the department suggested including a consumer opt-out provision to preserve choice and affordability.
The department will also consider requiring insurers to offer an optional OEM parts endorsement that consumers could purchase when obtaining or renewing coverage.
The report also raised questions about the extent to which insurers influence repairs through DRPs, estimating systems and parts sourcing requirements.

DFR found that DRPs can provide shops with customer referrals and offer consumers access to facilities evaluated by insurers. However, the programs can also give insurers greater influence over labor rates, parts selection and repair procedures.
The department noted that DRP agreements may affect the broader repair marketplace when nonparticipating shops accept insurer-established rates or estimates to remain competitive.

DFR plans to explore regulatory changes intended to preserve consumer choice and prevent insurer interference with necessary repair procedures unless a disagreement is based on legitimate technical issues evaluated by qualified representatives.
The department will also examine when insurer influence over repair decisions becomes a specific directive that could carry additional responsibility for repair costs or liability.
DFR found that consumer disclosures at the time an auto insurance policy is purchased are limited and often difficult to understand.
The department is considering additional disclosures at the time of purchase and when claims are filed, potentially through a consumer bill of rights.

The report also identified inconsistent insurer practices involving betterment deductions, which reduce claim payments when replacement parts are considered to improve a vehicle’s condition beyond its pre-loss state.

According to DFR, half of the responding insurers had no specific betterment procedures, and some applied deductions to third-party claimants even when those motorists were not responsible for the collision.
The department recommends adding betterment standards to Regulation I-79-2, potentially drawing from NAIC model language.
While the report identifies opportunities to strengthen consumer protections and improve repair reimbursement practices, DFR cautioned that regulatory changes could affect insurance affordability.
The department retained actuarial consulting firm Oliver Wyman to evaluate how hypothetical increases in collision repair labor rates and total loss valuations might affect insurance premiums.

Under the scenarios examined, labor rate increases of 10% to 40% could produce estimated premium increases ranging from 1.2% to 14.9%, depending on the proportion of insured vehicle damage and theft costs attributable to labor.
Separately, increases in total loss valuations of 10% to 30% could result in estimated premium increases ranging from 1% to 8.9%.
The report emphasized that these are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts of the effects of the department’s specific recommendations.

DFR also noted that Vermont has a competitive automobile insurance market, with more than 70 insurers offering private passenger coverage and premiums historically ranking among the lowest nationally.
However, the department warned that affordability pressures remain a concern, particularly as the state’s estimated uninsured motorist rate has risen above 10% since 2021.
The report represents a significant examination of the relationship between insurers, collision repair facilities and consumers in Vermont.
Its recommendations focus primarily on revising existing insurance regulations, strengthening disclosure requirements and establishing more consistent standards for claims handling.

For collision repairers, the most consequential proposals involve labor rate methodology, supplement processing deadlines, in-person appraisal requirements, aftermarket parts disclosures and insurer influence over repair decisions.

The department’s findings also underscore the challenges facing independent repair facilities as vehicle complexity increases and shops assume additional administrative responsibilities associated with insurance claims.

Although DFR did not recommend establishing a mandatory minimum collision repair labor rate, it concluded that the current regulatory framework needs greater clarity to address disagreements over repair costs and claims practices.

The report’s recommendations are not themselves new laws or binding regulatory changes. Any proposed amendments would require further action through the applicable state regulatory or legislative process.

articles.title: How Cam Designs Are Meeting More Specialized Demands
articles.author: Greg Jones

paras.en: Picking a camshaft used to involve a simple flip through a catalog to find a grind that matched your basic engine specs. Today, off-the-shelf cams still make sense for many applications, but more specialized engine combinations are pushing builders toward more custom solutions. Experts attribute this shift to a handful of factors.

Nick Norris of Callies says the move away from “one-size-fits-most” cams is largely due to combinations becoming too specialized. The same basic engine, he notes, can be naturally aspirated, turbocharged, positive-displacement supercharged, or run with nitrous, and each can require a very different approach to valve timing.

“Better EFI, data acquisition and simulation have also changed what we can evaluate,” Norris says. “We can look at boost, backpressure, converter behavior, engine acceleration, and other data and design around what the vehicle actually needs. Instead of asking only what cam will make the most power, we can ask where we need the torque and how we want that power delivered.”

All of this has changed how Norris and other top manufacturers look at valvetrain development. While cam specs and events have traditionally been referenced to what’s happening at the lobe, “for the past couple of years I’ve been retraining myself to think more about the events at the valve,” he says. “After all, that’s what the engine sees.”

That shift – from designing around the camshaft itself to designing around what the valve actually does – is a big part of where cam development is headed. It also helps explain why manufacturers are moving beyond basic specs like lobe separation angle (LSA) and taking a more complete, system-level approach to the valvetrain.

Why exactly is the market evolving this way? One important driver, according to Bobby Biancaniello of Cam Motion, is “the ability to have a camshaft spec’d for your exact build and ground and shipped to you in one week’s time.”

While Cam Motion’s off-the-shelf grinds will work for almost any late-model application, he notes, when you start changing things like runner lengths on intakes, incorporating power adders, or adding displacement by lengthening the stroke, “it’s easier to make them exactly what they need with a custom grind than having a catalog with thousands of options” that can just end up complicating the selection process.

Another reason for this changing dynamic is the role of modern technology and tuning. Nic Woods of Clay Smith Cams explains that until about 10-15 years ago, EFI was a major headache for cam manufacturers, and “there were only a few guys in the country who really knew how to dial in performance cams and get them tuned and mapped correctly for the air-fuel ratio at idle.”
But now, with the rapid evolution of ECU technology and how well these systems communicate with the O2 sensors, today’s self-learning systems can better accommodate more aggressive performance cams.

“We don’t really have to recommend cams differently for fuel-injected platforms anymore,” Woods says. “We can give them the right cam, and if the guy doesn’t know how to tune it, the fuel injection can self-learn and map the fuel correctly.”

Charlie Westcott of Militia Racing Products points to manufacturing technology and material advances as additional factors influencing the market. He says many traditional cam cores are designed to cover a wide range of applications, which can create challenges when they’re machined and heat-treated.

By comparison, tool-steel cores (like S7) are high-strength throughout and can be manufactured more efficiently without some of the heat-treating and coating steps that materials like 8620 or 9310 would require.

“I can make a camshaft – from a phone call to the finished product – in about three days,” Westcott says. “Those three days are only because I’m waiting for the heat treat to come back. Whereas if you’re doing these other cams, you have to send them out to get copper-coated, then send them out again for heat treatment after you mill them. It’s a big time suck. I prefer getting things done quickly for people.”

Of course, to get a custom camshaft recommendation, certain information must be collected. Norris says the engine’s cubic inches, rpm range, cylinder heads, and application will get the Callies team in the ballpark. But choosing the actual profiles requires more detail.

“We’ll look at the weights of the valvetrain components and the overall stiffness of the system based on things like pushrod dimensions, rocker ratios and material, and the rest of the valvetrain configuration,” Norris says.
The spring package is another big consideration. If a customer has one they’re happy with, Norris and his team will go over the specs to make sure it’s compatible with the profiles they’ve chosen.

“If we’re starting from scratch, the spring and lobe need to be considered together rather than treating the spring as something that gets selected after the cam,” he notes. “Ultimately, the basic engine information helps determine the valve events and general cam specifications, while the details of the valvetrain help determine how aggressive the lobe profiles can be and still maintain control through the intended rpm range.”

Biancaniello agrees that when deciding on the best camshaft for a particular application, “it’s important for the cam guy to know as much as possible about the setup.” That means customers need to be as clear and up front as possible about their goals and how they plan to use the vehicle. Why? Because two builds that look virtually the same can require two very different cams.

As an example, he points to a turbocharged LS 5.3L with a set of 62mm turbos. In one case, the engine is being used in a streetcar with a tight converter, air conditioning, power brakes, and no transbrake. This customer wants very quick spool-up, a broad powerband, a 6,500-rpm ceiling, and 700-plus horsepower.

“That setup will have much different specs than the identical engine/turbos going into a drag race-only application with a transbrake and a converter that flashes 6,200-plus rpm and gets run to 8,000 rpm max on much higher boost levels with a goal of 1,200-plus hp,” he says.
Norris offers a similar assessment, making note of pressure conditions and the fact that the same boost level with two different turbo systems can produce very different exhaust backpressure.

“That affects how I approach exhaust timing and overlap,” Norris explains. “The engine specifications may look nearly identical on paper, but what the vehicle needs from the engine can lead to two very different camshafts.”

Woods, too, leaves no stone unturned when gathering information, wanting to know the compression, what cylinder head is being used, the flow numbers, the type of intake manifold, components in the bottom end, and more.

“We need to have some idea of whose brand piston is in there so we can get a good estimate of how much valve clearance we have and how much camshaft we can actually put in before he has a problem,” Woods says.

Once the specs are covered, it’s time to discuss the vehicle and its intended use, which gives manufacturers an idea of rpm range and where a customer wants power and torque to occur. “Some of these conversations can take five minutes; some can take two hours,” Woods admits. “At the end of the day, the cam is the same price, but a company has to be willing to put in that extra time to make sure the customer gets the exact right cam for his application.”

Westcott, whose customers include Pro Line Racing and Noonan Race Engineering, among others, sees plenty of unorthodox projects as well. His work has covered everything from a one-of-a-kind 1969 455-style Pontiac engine with a single overhead cam to a four-valve-per-cylinder, small block Oldsmobile W-30 (one of only two ever made) to an inline six-cylinder Holden race engine from Australia and a set of John Deere tractor pulling cams. At this point, it’s safe to say almost nothing is out of bounds.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Even so, Westcott still gets calls where he has to steer people away from potential trouble. One of the most common mistakes he encounters is customers focusing too heavily on aggressive lobe profiles to try to maximize area under the curve.

“I always say, you can’t make an engine good with the camshaft,” he states. “The camshaft, in my mind, is like the conductor of the orchestra. You’ve got your cylinder heads and your manifold, and your induction system is probably the most important thing. It really sets the rpm band for the engine. The camshaft has to match that stuff, so the camshaft comes last in the party.”

In other words, a cam can’t compensate for an engine combo that won’t support the desired rpm or power level. “You can’t take a stock small-block Chevy 350 and change the cam and think you’re going to make power at 10,000 rpm,” he adds. “That’s just not going to do it.”
Instead, he says, builders should focus on getting the entire combination right rather than trying to make up for shortcomings with an overly aggressive camshaft.

“I have to talk guys out of trying to make aggressive lobes because they think they need to square up the lobes to make the engine good,” Westcott says. “I tell them, you need to fix your heads and make the cam smooth. That way you’re not beating up parts.”

An overly aggressive cam can create unnecessary stress throughout the valvetrain. “If you have to get so aggressive that you’re beating up stuff, that’s never good,” he says. “If you’ve got a jackhammer for an engine, you want the engine to be nice and smooth and not have any problems. Work on the induction system.”

Another common mistake is simply going too large on duration. “You’re better off being 5 degrees short than 5 degrees big,” he says. “Everybody wants to have the cam be too big, but they’ll typically run better if they’re smaller than if they’re bigger.”

For Biancaniello, the biggest sticking point is unquestionably LSA. He says engine builders will often request a cam with a specific LSA and little else, expecting him to fill in the blanks. He has to remind them that LSA is only one part of the equation.

“Duration and centerlines are equally important pieces to that puzzle,” he says. “We need to choose the correct valve timing the setup wants,” adding that he encourages builders to reference Cam Motion’s cam timing calculator to better understand how changes in cam specs affect the engine’s behavior.

“I can make a camshaft ‘work’ with the LSA you might think is ideal for the setup,” Biancaniello says, “but the more ideal approach would have been picking the best open and close timing and letting the duration/LSA and centerlines fall wherever they fall to make those events timed where you want them.”

Norris tabs a common mistake as choosing a cam primarily from duration at .050” lift. While he notes that’s an important number, “it doesn’t tell you where the valve events occur or how the valve gets from the seat to peak lift and back.”

He also warns against concentrating too much on duration and lobe separation and overlooking the individual valve events. Intake closing, exhaust opening and the amount and location of overlap can have a major effect on where the engine makes torque and how it responds.

“The valvetrain also has to be considered,” Norris adds. “A lobe may look ideal from an airflow standpoint but be too aggressive for the lifter, rocker, valve, and spring combination. Making the cam more aggressive doesn’t help if the valvetrain becomes unstable before the engine reaches its intended rpm.”

As racing classes and enthusiast segments continue to become more specialized, application-specific camshaft development will undoubtedly progress in kind. Biancaniello expects the industry to head “down a further rabbit hole of constant testing, R&D and real-world data” to keep pace with the seemingly endless introduction of new segments and rulebooks on the competition side.

Norris sees the next step as combining traditional cam design with more detailed analysis of the complete valvetrain. Duration, lift and valve events will always be important, he says, “but we’re increasingly able to evaluate velocity, acceleration, jerk, radius of curvature and frequency content along with actual valve motion from Spintron testing.”

The long-term goal, then, is to put that data to work earlier in the cycle. “The ability to predict if and when the valvetrain will become unstable in software, verify it through Spintron testing and ultimately validate it on the dyno would take the development process to the next level,” Norris states.

Woods raises an interesting point about the future, and something he would like to see become more commonplace in the market: moving toward validated systems to prevent premature failures, especially in high-end builds.

“You get into those specialty racing applications and you test your lobe designs on a Spintron,” he says. “You have this rocker arm, this spring, this retainer, this pushrod, and this head, and then you sell the cam by itself – how does that make sense? It’s almost like you can only buy this cam with what we tested it with.

“That’s something I think the industry is really lacking: telling the customer that these lobes are specific for drag-racing applications, and you have to have this rocker, this spring, this retainer, and this diameter pushrod with this wall thickness. Otherwise, the results may vary. When it gets to those levels of application, you have to have the system. If one piece of that system isn’t in place, the likelihood of premature failure is evident. It’s impossible for it not to be.”

The bottom line is that off-the-shelf camshafts certainly have their place, but the direction of the industry is clear. As engine combinations get more specialized and manufacturers zero in on what’s happening at the valve, the cam is becoming less of an isolated component and increasingly one piece in a complete valvetrain system.

articles.title: How OE Tire Fitments Influence Replacement Tire Sales
articles.author: Denise Koeth

paras.en: An original equipment (OE) tire fitment can influence a customer’s next tire purchase years after a vehicle leaves the factory. Aaron Neumann, head of the Nexen Tire America Technical Center, estimates that around 30% of drivers request the same tire or brand when shopping for replacements. Among luxury vehicle owners, he says more than half choose the same brand.

For tire dealers, that familiarity creates an opportunity to turn OE tire fitments into replacement sales. But making the right recommendation requires understanding why automakers select particular tires, which customers want to preserve their vehicle’s original performance and when another tire might better meet their needs.
Neumann explains how OE partnerships influence consumer purchasing decisions and what dealers should consider when recommending replacement tires.

An OE tire can begin taking shape two to three years before its intended vehicle even reaches the market. Tiremakers earn an OE fitment on a vehicle through a multi-year, collaborative engineering and testing process with the auto manufacturer long before the vehicle goes into production.

“There is a high bar to earning OE fitment,” says Aaron Neumann, head of Nexen Tire America Technical Center. “Technically, a tire manufacturer has to prove they have a highly controlled production process with robust quality systems that pass very stringent audits. They also must have the technical capability to meet performance targets at the leading edge of tire technology, which is generally only within reach for Tier 1 and 2 manufacturers. Commercially, they need to show a top-level financial rating and logistically, need to show a 100% on-time global supply chain.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Neumann says many Hyundai, Kia, Ram and Jeep vehicles in the United States feature Nexen tires.

“Two fitments we’re particularly excited about right now are the Jeep Wrangler and the new Jeep Recon,” he says. “We are also very proud of our Porsche Panamera and Cayenne fitments. Those programs are good examples of the range of capabilities required in OE development. The performance targets for a Porsche are different from those of a Jeep, but in both cases the tire has to be engineered as part of the vehicle rather than treated as an off-the-shelf component.”
For a tire manufacturer, the rigorous process is worth it for both the added business and increased brand awareness.
While Nexen does see an increase in replacement sales for sizes with OE fitments, quantifying brand awareness is a little more difficult, according to Neumann.

“There are so many new brands in the market, and customers only need to think about tires once every few years, but OE creates familiarity over the entire ownership period,” he says. “Someone may see Nexen on their own vehicle, on a neighbor’s SUV or a spare OE Nexen Roadian HTX2 on the back of a Jeep Wrangler during their morning commute every day. They may not consciously think about it at the time, but that exposure helps make the brand familiar. That recognition matters when it becomes time to replace tires.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That tendency to stick with an OE tire varies by vehicle segment and by what customers expect from their replacement tires.

“Understandably, luxury or performance owners are more sensitive to maintaining the way the vehicle was engineered to drive, so they place more value on staying with the OE brand or specification,” he says. “At the other end of the market, a value-oriented consumer may be more willing to compare brands based on price, mileage or another practical need.”
How OE Tire Fitments Influence Replacement Sales

When recommending replacement tires, ask customers what performance characteristics they want from their vehicles. Ask whether customers liked their OE tires and what driving conditions they regularly face. Then determine whether the OE fitment or another product is the best choice.

For luxury and performance vehicle owners, Neumann suggests considering which characteristics the driver wants to preserve, including steering response, ride quality, noise levels, braking and handling.

“Enthusiasts can be similar, although they may also be more willing to move away from the exact OE tire if they are deliberately trying to change a particular performance characteristic,” he adds. “That’s where understanding the customer’s priorities becomes important.

“Generally, OE specification carries more weight as vehicles become more specialized and customers become more sensitive to how the vehicle performs. That can include luxury cars, sports cars, performance SUVs and increasingly EVs, where factors such as rolling resistance, noise, vehicle weight and range can all make tire selection more noticeable.”

However, Neumann explains that in these instances, OE is not automatically the best replacement choice simply because of the vehicle type or price point. “The better question is whether the customer wants to preserve the original balance of performance or change it,” he notes.
From a customer’s point of view, it depends less on the vehicle and more on what they need from their tires.

“If they are happy with the OE tire’s performance, then replace them like for like,” Neumann says. “If they live in snow country, then they should upgrade to a tire marked with a three-peak mountain snowflake symbol. Now, if they do a lot of miles and would like better treadwear, then look for tires with longer treadwear warranties. If they have a truck and want to upgrade the appearance, look for a more aggressive A/T or R/T tire.”

He explains that when the switch is made from OE tires to a different product, there will be a trade-off, “perhaps 2 mpg of fuel economy or a little bit more tire noise,” but that many people think these trade-offs are worth making.
“I’m an advocate for teaching consumers about tire performance and trade-offs so they can make educated decisions when buying tires,” Neumann says.

articles.title: NAPA Apprentice Program Builds a New Path Into the Service Bay
articles.author: NAPA

paras.en: As repair shops across the country struggle to recruit qualified technicians, the NAPA Auto Care Apprentice Program offers participating businesses a structured way to develop new talent inside their own service bays.

More than 700 NAPA Auto Care centers nationwide participate in the program, which combines technical education, hands-on experience and mentorship. Its mission is to educate and cultivate the next generation of automotive repair professionals by providing a broad learning experience that combines online and classroom training.

For shop owners, the program offers an alternative to waiting for experienced technicians to appear in an increasingly competitive labor market. A participating shop can identify someone with the right attitude and work ethic, then help that person build technical skills through a defined training path.

“NAPA is committed to finding solutions that address the national shortage of skilled automotive technicians,” said Jason Rainey, vice president of Auto Care. “Our apprenticeship program is one of several key NAPA initiatives that help pave the way for young people to launch long and fruitful careers in our industry.”

The NAPA Apprentice Program uses a nine-stage curriculum designed to give participants a broad understanding of the systems and components found on modern vehicles. Most apprentices can complete the program in two years or less.

However, the curriculum is competency-based rather than tied strictly to a calendar. Apprentices can progress through each stage at a pace that matches their learning style and demonstrated abilities. A participant who quickly masters a subject can move forward, while someone who needs additional practice can spend more time developing that competency.
Training is 100% technical and is delivered through several formats:
- Classroom training videos exclusive to the Apprentice Program provide in-depth instruction from experienced master technicians.
- NAPA Autotech classes offer instructor-led training taught by experienced ASE Master Certified instructors.
- Autotech eLearning provides web-based instruction targeting specific systems, procedures and diagnostic topics.
- Hands-on training allows apprentices to apply what they have learned while working in the shop under the guidance of a mentor.

This combination helps connect classroom theory with real repairs. Apprentices do not just learn how a component operates; they also gain experience inspecting, testing and servicing that component on vehicles.

The curriculum will continue to evolve as vehicle technology and industry standards change. Planned enhancements include updated training modules and specialized certification options covering emerging service areas, giving apprentices additional opportunities for career advancement.

Apprentices earn the work experience requirement for three Automotive Service Excellence certifications as they advance through the program: Maintenance and Light Repair (G1), Suspension and Steering (A4), and Brakes (A5). They also gain the practical know-how to pass the EPA Section 609 refrigerant recovery and recycling credential test administered through ASE.

That distinction is important: G1, A4 and A5 are ASE professional certifications, while Section 609 is an EPA-required credential for technicians who service motor-vehicle air-conditioning systems. Together, these credentials provide outside validation of the knowledge and skills developed during the apprenticeship.

Because the program is registered with the U.S. Department of Labor, graduates also finish with a nationally recognized journey-level credential in automotive repair. This gives apprentices evidence of completing a structured combination of education and supervised on-the-job training.

The program provides the curriculum and training materials, but its success inside a repair facility depends heavily on the shop’s involvement. An apprentice needs an experienced technician who can explain procedures, demonstrate good work habits, supervise repairs and provide constructive feedback.

“We need their mentorship, their participation,” said Hannah Klausman, account marketing manager for Auto Care. “We want to support them by providing the materials for their technicians to go through this program, but we need their buy-in by having them provide a mentor and really put their time into taking a chance on these new technicians.”

For a shop owner, that requires a real commitment. Mentoring can temporarily affect the productivity of an experienced technician, especially during an apprentice’s first months. The potential return is a technician trained around the shop’s procedures, quality standards and culture.

The program can also create a clearer career ladder. Instead of hiring someone as an entry-level employee with no defined next step, a shop can show the apprentice how training, demonstrated competencies and certifications lead to greater responsibilities.

“The success of the apprentice program is a reflection not only of the investment NAPA has made but also of its collaboration with Auto Care centers across the country,” said Ryan Ouellette, director of strategic accounts at NAPA. “We are committed to developing future professionals at NAPA, and we look forward to continuing to educate and support the talent in the industry.”
Applicants must be at least 17 years old. Applicants who are 17 require written parental consent, and there is no maximum age.

Previous professional repair experience is not the program’s defining qualification. Shops should look for candidates who have a positive attitude, arrive ready to work and take initiative beyond their assigned tasks.

Successful apprentices must also be able to build relationships. Automotive repair is increasingly collaborative, particularly when diagnostic information, specialized equipment and technical knowledge must be shared among technicians. An apprentice must be willing to ask questions, accept coaching and learn from the people around them.
Most importantly, candidates need to embrace continuous learning. Vehicle technology does not stand still, and neither can a technician’s education.

For aspiring technicians, the program provides an opportunity to learn the trade without taking on the expense of a traditional trade-school program. Apprentices receive a paycheck while learning in an operating repair facility, and the training itself is provided at no cost to the participant.
Additional information about the program is available at NAPA Auto Care Training.
Sidebar: Addressing the Cost of a Technician’s First Tools

Tools represent one of the largest entry barriers for a new automotive technician. Even a basic professional set can require a substantial investment before the technician earns a full professional wage.

To help address that barrier, Carlyle Tools developed an Apprentice Set containing professional-quality tools considered essential for a new technician’s career. NAPA Auto Care makes the exclusive set, which has a stated retail value of $6,566, available for participating Auto Care centers to purchase for their apprentices.

Providing or helping finance an appropriate starter set can make a shop’s apprenticeship opportunity more attractive. It also helps ensure that the apprentice begins with tools capable of withstanding daily professional use.

articles.title: Hella Launches Commercial Vehicle Brake Pads
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: Hella Aftermarket is introducing brake pads for trucks, buses, and trailers, the company’s first offering in the commercial vehicle sector. The products are now available worldwide.

“We are starting with brake pads for trucks, buses, and trailers and will gradually expand the range,” says Dr. Marcel Wiedmann, head of the global aftermarket business at Forvia Hella. “Building on our established brake offering for passenger cars, we are now transferring our expertise to the commercial vehicle sector.”
Hella is launching an initial portfolio of 58 references, covering a range of applications and model variants, the company said.

The new program is designed for the high thermal and mechanical loads in heavy-duty applications. Each brake lining features matched friction materials to support braking performance, service life, and comfort in daily operation. Where necessary, linings are supplied with application-specific accessories.
All brake pads are tested and certified according to international safety and quality standards, including ECE R90.

articles.title: Volvo Trucks Sponsors ATA’s America’s Road Team in 2027
articles.author: Jason Morgan

paras.en: Volvo Trucks North America will serve as the exclusive sponsor of the American Trucking Associations’ America’s Road Team for 2027. This is its 25th consecutive year supporting the program. The announcement was made during the American Trucking Associations’ 2026 Management Conference & Exhibition in Charlotte.
Road Team Captains Bring Safety Experience to Public Outreach

America’s Road Team selects professional drivers as captains based on their exemplary safety records and ability to speak about the industry. There are currently 92 active Captains. Because many stay involved well past their two-year terms, the roster has grown into a standing corps of ambassadors. Captains have logged approximately 428 million safe driving miles over the 25 years of Volvo’s sponsorship. Additionally, 213 million of those by the 92 Captains active today.

The Captains’ experience behind the wheel forms the foundation of their work as trusted voices for the trucking industry. They testify before lawmakers, run ride-alongs for policymakers and reporters, and talk to students at career fairs. ATA counts more than 230 safety events since 2019, and the program has reached an estimated 2.5 million people.
Volvo VNL 860 Takes the Mobile Classroom Nationwide

The newly selected Captains will tour the country in a fully equipped, all-new Volvo VNL 860. It will transport the ATA Interstate One mobile classroom to events and communities nationwide. Volvo Trucks’ all-new Volvo VNL touts a next-generation suite of digital and mechanical safety systems. This includes advanced driver assistance and occupant protection. These technologies help safeguard lives and reduce the risk of serious injuries in an accident.
The full article can be found on fleetequipmentmag.com.

articles.title: Allison Transmission Unifies Brands Following Acquisition
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Allison Transmission Holdings Inc. announced its new brand structure following its acquisition of Dana Inc.’s Off-Highway Drive & Motion Systems business earlier this year. Effective immediately, the company’s enterprise brand is Allison. Its Allison Transmission and Allison Off-Highway Drive & Motion Systems business units will operate under the unified Allison name. The change also encompasses their combined product portfolio.
Allison Transmission Retains Established Product Brands

Allison will retain established product brands within the acquired off-highway business unit, including Spicer, Brevini, GWB, Fairfield and Graziano. The company will continue to develop, sell and service these products alongside those from the Allison Transmission business unit. Customers, distributors and dealers across both business units will continue to receive support for existing products and parts.

“Our products have a long history, earning the trust of customers over decades. Much of what they value about Allison is embodied in the product brands themselves,” said David Graziosi, Allison chair, president and CEO. “By uniting all of our product brands under Allison, we communicate a consistent strategy and promise to keep the essential industries our customers serve moving forward with confidence.”
Allison to Showcase Unified Portfolio at bauma China

Allison will showcase its unified brand in November at bauma China, a construction and mining machinery industry event. The company will display products spanning the full driveline, including axles, transmissions and driveshafts. The exhibit will highlight the combined portfolio available to existing and prospective customers.

articles.title: LKQ Names Salvatore Abbate President and CEO
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: LKQ Corp. announced that its board of directors has appointed Salvatore “Sal” Abbate president and CEO, effective Dec. 15, 2026. He will succeed Justin Jude, who will leave the company effective immediately. LKQ has established an interim office of the CEO until Abbate assumes his new role. The office consists of John Mendel, board chairman, and Sue Gove, chair of LKQ’s audit committee. They will work closely with LKQ’s leadership teams and management to oversee operations during the transition.
LKQ Appoints Experienced Distribution Executive

Abbate brings more than three decades of experience leading large, complex distribution and industrial businesses. As CEO of Veritiv Corp., he led a significant transformation of the company. Its share price increased more than 13-fold during his tenure. The transformation culminated in Veritiv’s $2.6 billion sale to Clayton, Dubilier & Rice in 2023.

Before becoming CEO, Abbate served as Veritiv’s chief operating officer and chief commercial officer. Earlier, Abbate held senior leadership roles at Andersen Windows & Doors, Solutia Inc. and Armstrong World Industries. Solutia is now part of Eastman Chemical Co. His responsibilities spanned sales, marketing, distribution, logistics, manufacturing, strategy and process improvement.
Abbate Brings Operational and Supply Chain Experience

Abbate’s experience aligns with LKQ’s strategic and operational priorities. He has led high-volume, multisite distribution businesses where pricing, procurement and supply chain discipline are critical to performance. He also has led portfolio transformations focused on margin improvement and cash generation.

Abbate brings public company and international experience. He currently serves on the board of ArcBest. He holds a bachelor’s degree in industrial engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology. He also holds an MBA from Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

“After a thorough search, the Board concluded that Sal is the right leader for LKQ at this moment,” said John Mendel, Chairman of the Board. “He is a disciplined operator and people-centered leader, who has transformed a complex distribution business, improved margins and created significant value for shareholders. Sal brings the operating rigor, commercial instincts and sense of urgency we need to sharpen execution across our businesses and unlock the full potential of LKQ. On behalf of the Board, I also want to thank Justin for his years of service and contributions to LKQ.”

articles.title: NAPA Academy Provides New Training Resources
articles.author: Doug Kaufman

paras.en: Running a successful parts store requires more than knowing which part fits which vehicle. It takes effective inventory management, dependable delivery service, employees who understand customers’ needs and a manager who can connect everyday decisions to the store’s financial performance.

NAPA is giving independent store owners new resources to develop those capabilities through NAPA Academy, extending training developed for its company-owned stores to independent businesses. The program was introduced during the 2026 NAPA Store Owner and Field Sales Meeting, held Sept. 21-24 in Atlanta. The initial offering focuses on store managers, combining short online courses with a downloadable resource guide designed to help translate training into daily practice.

Introducing the program, Cassie Bell, NAPA’s senior vice president of HR, said the expansion supports the company’s Drive 2030 strategy and its investment in people. Although owners have requested training for several positions, she said store managers were a logical starting point.

“We believe fundamentally that the store manager is critical to obtaining consistent customer service, to building the teams and driving those operational performances inside of our stores,” Bell said.
The program’s development began with a practical question: What do successful employees and stores do differently?

Jesse Parrish, NAPA’s director of learning and development, said the Academy worked with teams across the organization to identify the knowledge, skills and behaviors that define excellence in specific roles. NAPA partnered with industry professionals to turn those findings into training, reference materials and learning pathways.

By observing high-performing managers and market directors in top-performing stores, the team identified the practices and strategies driving their success. Those real-world insights became the foundation for new training programs designed to help others apply proven strategies throughout the organization.

For store operations, the resulting framework has four areas of emphasis: driving financial results, leading and developing teams, enabling operational excellence and delivering exceptional customer service.

Those areas address responsibilities ranging from understanding store performance and building improvement plans to coaching employees, managing inventory, optimizing delivery service and building customer loyalty.
The team documented those practices in how-to guides, training courses and tools intended to help other stores apply them.
The online courses generally take 10 to 20 minutes to complete. Owners can take the courses themselves or assign them to employees, allowing training to address specific development needs.

Although the first offering centers on store management, its usefulness extends to other positions. Parrish pointed to customer service lessons, including effective phone conversations, as examples of content relevant to counter employees.
“It is not just limited to the store manager,” he said. “While the content’s focused on them, there are relevant courses here for others that may be frontline workers working the counter.”

That connection matters because a store’s customer experience depends on both management decisions and individual employee interactions. Training managers to coach their teams complements instruction that helps counter professionals better serve wholesale and retail customers.

The second major resource is a downloadable store manager guide. It outlines the role’s responsibilities, key functions and performance metrics, with linked how-to guidance covering subjects such as budgeting, performance management, customer service and root cause analysis.
Parrish described its purpose in everyday terms: helping employees understand “how do you do the work on a Tuesday morning at nine o’clock?”

The training framework recognizes three proficiency levels: foundation, advanced and mastery. Foundation focuses on performing a job independently and effectively. Advanced emphasizes consistently meeting performance targets and helping others succeed. Mastery involves anticipating opportunities, leading broader improvements and consistently exceeding targets.
That structure provides a development path for employees with different experience levels, from someone entering a management role to an established leader seeking to improve store performance.

Participation is voluntary, Parrish emphasized, with independent owners able to use the resources as they see fit within their businesses. The materials are intended to remain within the NAPA family. NAPA also is exploring how to tailor resources further to independent owners’ needs.

Bell encouraged owners to access the content, develop a plan for using it and return regularly as materials are updated. She also asked them to share feedback about missing resources or opportunities for improvement.

“If you need something more, you need something different, something’s not working, whatever that looks like, please reach back out to us,” Bell said. “We are only as good as the feedback we’re receiving from you.”

articles.title: How Simplification Can Create New Capacity for Growth
articles.author: Darcy Curran

paras.en: In the automotive aftermarket, growth is often associated with adding more: more products, more inventory, more suppliers and more resources. However, adding more doesn’t always lead to growth. In fact, adding more can introduce unnecessary complexity, making growth more difficult. The most successful businesses understand where they create the greatest value and have the discipline to direct resources toward those priorities.

No business can excel at everything. The most important strategic decision is often determining what not to do. Companies should first define what they want to be known for and how they can deliver distinctive value to customers. That requires discipline: investing in the right areas, focusing on the highest priorities, and stopping work that no longer advances the strategy.

Without this focus, complexity can surface quickly, and companies can wind up working too hard on the wrong things. The real cost isn’t limited to the time or dollars spent managing the complexity. More importantly, it includes potential growth opportunities missed because resources are not directed correctly.

Inventory management is one area where this can be seen. Healthy inventory turns consistently for suppliers and distributors, whereas chronically slow-moving inventory can signal that resources are not creating enough value for customers. Even inventory that isn’t moving still requires dollars to acquire, manage, store and move through the operation, and these costs can add up quickly, especially when the product isn’t generating meaningful sales.

As an important proactive action, suppliers and distributors should consistently review inventory investment and turns to help identify which products are creating value and where resources can be better focused to help drive growth.

The purchase price is easy to measure, and too often, businesses try to sell for the most and buy for the least. But greater value can come from understanding what partners need and where their challenges exist.

For distributors, there’s also value in building deeper relationships with a focused group of suppliers. During periods of supply disruption or elevated demand, manufacturers and other suppliers naturally prioritize their most important customers. These relationships create opportunities to support each other’s businesses better while establishing mutual trust and confidence.

In one supplier relationship, we learned a partner was looking to borrow money to fund an expansion. We had already planned to extend our contract, but by executing the agreement earlier, we gave our partner longer-term, predictable business, reducing their risk to their lender and allowing them to borrow at a lower rate. This early extension allowed both sides to get what they needed without simply negotiating over another percentage point on price.

The critical learning from this example is the importance of building relationships that are strategic rather than simply transactional. The most important question is: How can we change the way we do business to benefit both sides beyond the purchase order’s value? When distributors and suppliers understand each other’s businesses well enough to answer this question, the relationship can become stronger and create better economics for both sides.

Simplification also extends to how distributors serve their customers. By providing more flexibility in terms of how customers purchase and receive products, distributors can help customers manage their inventory more efficiently while maximizing their dollars and warehouse space.

Consider the difference between buying a case and a pallet: rather than putting significantly more cash into inventory up front, smaller quantities and more frequent replenishment can help align inventory more closely with demand.

That same principle can extend across the broader supplier relationship. When customers can access more of what they need in smaller quantities and combine categories into fewer shipments, they can simplify ordering and receiving, turn inventory faster and manage working capital and space more effectively.

Delivering that value also requires distributors to make smart decisions behind the scenes, specifically where distribution centers are located, how products move through them, and how far they travel to customers. All these decisions affect cost and reliability, specifically when distributing heavy, low-cost products. By adopting a more strategically positioned distribution network, distributors can reduce costs and improve service without increasing customer charges.

For Highline Warren, we start with a simple question: What do we want to be known for? We want customers to know that they can rely on us to deliver products on time and in full. Consistently delivering on those priorities builds credibility and can make a supplier more integral to the customer’s process, turning focus into a foundation for growth.

Understanding where a business creates value can also help identify its next growth opportunity. For suppliers and distributors, one of the easiest, fastest and most economical ways to grow is to sell existing products to existing customers. The relationship is already established, the supplier understands the customer, and the customer already knows the value the supplier provides. From there, a business should look at the broader market and consider how products or categories it already carries can help address another need.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: For example, a retailer may buy several product categories from one supplier while sourcing other products elsewhere, even though the same supplier already carries those products. The overlap creates an opportunity to grow by leveraging existing products and capabilities.

Growth frequently happens in concentric circles: first by strengthening existing relationships, then by expanding into adjacent opportunities that align with proven capabilities. Businesses that consistently deliver value earn the right to broaden those relationships over time.

Simplification isn’t simply about doing less. It is about being more deliberate and strategic about where a business puts its time, attention and resources, focusing on the areas that can drive meaningful growth.

Growth isn’t always about adding more; often, it comes from getting more from the products, capabilities and relationships a business has already established. Businesses disciplined enough to focus on this approach are better positioned to support customer needs, further strengthen relationships and create opportunities for mutual success.

articles.title: Mold gold cape: A 3,900-year-old accessory that's one of the finest examples of prehistoric goldwork ever found
articles.author: Kristina Killgrove

paras.en: Where it is from: Bryn yr Ellyllon (Goblins' Hill), Wales
When it was made: Circa 1900 to 1600 B.C.

In 1833, stone quarry workers discovered an ancient burial mound at Goblins' Hill near the town of Mold in Wales. At the center was a stone-lined grave that contained a fragmented skeleton and a gold, cape-like accessory that had been crushed over time. The Mold gold cape has a unique shape and style, and it is one of the finest examples of prehistoric goldwork ever found, according to the British Museum, where the artifact is on display.

The cape dates to Britain's Early Bronze Age (2500 to 1200 B.C.), a time that saw a metalworking revolution as artisans shifted from crafting flint tools to making weapons and jewelry out of gold, copper and bronze.

When the cape was originally unearthed, experts assumed that it had belonged to an ancient warrior, chief or religious leader, due to the spectacular design of the object, Benjamin Roberts, then curator for the European Bronze Age collections at the British Museum, told the BBC in 2010. But after the broken pieces of the cape were put back together, the small size of the artifact suggested it may have been worn by a woman or a child.

The Mold gold cape measures roughly 9.3 inches (23.5 centimeters) tall and 18.3 inches (46.5 cm) wide. It weighs about 1.2 pounds (560 grams) and was probably crafted from a single lump of gold about the size of a ping-pong ball.

The gold ingot was beaten incredibly thin, fashioned into a cape, and then embellished with decorations that mimicked beads or necklaces, according to the British Museum. Additionally, several hundred amber beads were found on the cape in the grave, which likely added to the gilded appearance of the accessory. Perforations around the neck opening suggest the cape originally had a lining made of leather or another perishable material that did not survive.

Because the gold cape, when worn, would restrict a person's upper arm movements, it may have been a ceremonial accessory that conferred religious authority and was worn only on special occasions. But experts are still unsure why the cape was buried in a grave. Nor can they confirm whether the person it was interred with was male or female, as the skeleton was not recovered by the quarry workers in the 19th century.

"The cape is unique — there is really nothing to compare it to in the whole of Europe," Roberts told the BBC. "This makes it more difficult to understand why it was made and what significance it had."

articles.title: Rare burial of elite toddler from pre-Inca culture discovered in Peru
articles.author: Margherita Bassi

paras.en: Archaeologists in Peru have found an elaborate 1,500-year-old tomb that may hold the remains of a high-status toddler from a pre-Inca civilization.
The burial, which is from the Moche culture, also contained vessels depicting prisoners with rope around each of their necks and a sculpture of a human-bird deity.

Moche (also known as Mochica) culture developed along the northern coast of what is now Peru from the third to the ninth century. They created agricultural lands in the region's desert landscape, and their archaeological record includes monumental temples, water canals, pottery, metallurgy, textiles and a distinctive form of art. The Moche didn't have a written language, but they left behind thousands of realistic portrait vessels, which are somewhat similar to the prisoner sculptors found in the toddler's burial.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In the newfound tomb, the team unearthed a small skeleton, which is likely the remains of a toddler who was, at most, 2 years old, Carlos Rengifo-Chunga, director of the University of Trujillo's Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project, told Live Science. The child's sex is unknown.

Rengifo-Chunga and his colleagues also found two copper objects in the burial: a mask-like disk covering the child's face, and a half-moon object on their feet. In addition, the burial contained 32 ceramic objects associated with Moche culture, including those depicting the prisoners and the deity.
The tomb was large compared to the child's small size, and could have easily held an adult, Rengifo-Chunga said. It dates to the sixth or seventh century, he added.

The team unearthed the tomb inside the Uhle Platform at the Huacas de Moche archaeological site in northern Peru. The Uhle Platform is a mausoleum, attached to the Huaca de la Luna temple, with a patio archaeologists call the Patio of the Serpents. Of the more than 80 burials previously uncovered there, the tomb represents the only known child to receive this sort of lavish burial.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The elaborate funerary treatment, including the use of copper, and the location of the tomb all suggest that the child belonged to an elite class of Moche society, Rengifo-Chunga said.

The two prisoner sculptures are associated with the "ritual of combat," a common theme in Moche art. In this sort of imagery, two warriors fight each other, and the loser is stripped of his clothes and weapons, tied around the neck with a rope and offered as a human sacrifice, Rengifo-Chunga said. The prisoners depicted on these two vessels were the losing warriors, and their presence in the burial of a child is rare.

"One would normally presume that these kinds of vessels represent something related to the deceased's life," Rengifo-Chunga said. For example, a vessel like this might signify that the individual took part in combat.
One of the ceramic objects depicts a presumed deity with human and bird features.
An archaeological team discovered a likely elite child burial at the Huacas de Moche archaeological site in Peru.
One of the two ceramics depicting prisoners that archaeologists found in the toddler's burial.

But a toddler couldn't have taken part in such an activity. In general, archaeologists wouldn't expect to see elements of an adult ritual in the burial of a child. "This expands our knowledge on Moche funerary practices," he added.

The sculpture of the presumed deity depicts a human body with bird wings and a bird tail, although for some scholars it might be interpreted as a god in transformation, Rengifo-Chunga said. The deity holds a square shield in one hand and a goblet in the other, and is flanked by two bird "assistants" wearing ceremonial garments.

Researchers will have to investigate whether the deity is a known Moche god, or a newfound addition to the pantheon. Either way, the object joins a contentious debate over whether the Moche pantheon consists of many gods, or just a few that can transform into many different versions, Rengifo-Chunga said.
The artifacts are now in the laboratories of the Santiago Uceda Castillo Museum in Peru, where they will undergo conservation treatment.
How much do you know about the first people to reach the Americas? Find out with our First Americans quiz.

Margherita is a trilingual freelance writer specializing in science and history writing with a particular interest in archaeology, palaeontology, astronomy and human behavior. She earned her BA from Boston College in English literature, ancient history and French, and her journalism MA from L'École Du Journalisme de Nice in International New Media Journalism. In addition to Live Science, her bylines include Smithsonian Magazine, Discovery Magazine, BBC Travel, Atlas Obscura and more.

articles.title: NASA's Swift observatory ends 22-year mission, will crash to Earth 'in the next few weeks'
articles.author: Brandon Specktor

paras.en: A pioneering NASA space telescope is no more. In sad news for Swifties everywhere, the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has officially ended its mission after more than 20 years of tracking the most powerful explosions in the universe since the Big Bang.

According to a NASA announcement, the Swift team shut down the telescope's science operations Tuesday (Oct. 20) after the observatory fell too low in its orbit to continue taking reliable measurements of the cosmos. In the coming weeks, Swift will drop even further, eventually passing a point of no return and taking a fiery plunge through Earth's atmosphere.

The observatory is the latest victim of intense solar activity, which increases the drag on satellites in Earth orbit and makes it harder for spacecraft to stay aloft. Swift has been losing altitude for a while, but the final straw came in August, when a costly mission to boost Swift's orbit with a private spacecraft failed, ending with the would-be rescue craft burning up in the atmosphere after a series of hardware malfunctions.

Swift is now beyond saving and, orbiting at just 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth, can no longer take reliable observations of space. NASA expects the spacecraft to break up upon reentry "in the next few weeks."

NASA knew Swift was in trouble when it went in; soon, it'll be lying on the cold hard ground. However, the Swift mission surpassed its goals by decades. According to NASA, the satellite launched in November 2004 on a primary mission intended to last just two years. In the end, Swift survived for 22 years, surpassing its intended lifespan by more than 10 times.

In that time, Swift made thousands of observations of exploding supernovas, intense gamma-ray bursts, and black-hole-related episodes of stellar destruction, contributing data to about 7,000 scientific papers, according to NASA.
- Gamma-ray bursts reveal largest structure in the universe is bigger and closer to Earth than we knew: 'The jury is still out on what it all means.'
- Did a NASA telescope really 'see' dark matter? Strange gamma-rays spark bold claims, but scientists urge caution
- Brightest gamma-ray burst ever detected defies explanation

Designed as a multiwavelength observatory, Swift watched the sky in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light that made it well suited to track the aftermath of powerful energy bursts. Its greatest asset, perhaps, was its rapid response time; if an explosion flashed somewhere in the sky, engineers could swivel Swift to study it within minutes, NASA said.

"Swift was designed as a satellite dedicated to studying gamma-ray bursts, outbursts that came and went so quickly that no one could target them with large telescopes to learn more," S. Bradley Cenko, the mission's principal investigator at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, said in the statement.

Swift's fast-acting observations "played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics," added Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA headquarters.

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. With more than 20 years of editorial experience, his writing has appeared in The Washington Post, Reader's Digest, CBS.com, the Richard Dawkins Foundation website and other outlets. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.
