articles.title: Rule Breaking Is Contagious. Just a Few Extreme Troublemakers Can Turn a Whole Group Into Rebels, Study Suggests

paras.en: Whether it’s driving above the speed limit or sneaking snacks from home into the movie theater, most people have broken a rule here and there. But how do other people’s behaviors influence your rule-breaking tendencies?

Researchers conducted behavioral tests with real people and simulations using their digital twins and found that just a few extreme troublemakers could ignite a full-blown revolt. The experiments, described in a study published October 21 in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B, don’t perfectly align with real-world contexts, but they do provide a glimpse at how rule-breaking can escalate.

“Prior research shows that rule violations and other antisocial behaviors can spread through social influence, but less is known about how the severity of violations shapes these dynamics,” the team writes in the study. “In many real-world settings, rule-breaking occurs in degrees, from minor infractions to major violations, and individuals may not only imitate others but sometimes exceed the violations they observe.”

To get a better understanding of these dynamics, the scientists recruited 750 online participants from the United States, about half of whom self-identified as Democrats and the other half as Republicans. It was a contentious time, just a week before the 2024 U.S. presidential election.

The participants were paid to observe a shooting star travel across a row of 100 squares on their screen and pick the brightest one. But there was a catch: The brightest square was always near the middle, but picking squares farther to the right increasingly netted them more cash.

Initially, around a fifth of the participants followed the rules every time, and another fifth of the participants were rule breakers. However, gaining insights about others’ behaviors shifted the results.

“Many people think of themselves as making sort of autonomous decisions, especially in these individualist cultures that we are from, like Netherlands, the U.K.,” study co-author Lucas Molleman, a social scientist at the University of Amsterdam, tells the Guardian’s Nicola Davis. “But in actual fact, in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing.”

Across several experiments, researchers told the participants whether another person had followed the rules or had committed a minor or major violation, and sometimes whether they were politically aligned. Rule-following rarely spread, but rule-breaking triggered a cascade, especially if done by a political comrade. Additionally, a tiny proportion of participants—4.4 percent—were true troublemakers, violating the rules beyond what was done by the rule-breaker whose response they knew about.
Fun fact: Social status and rule-breaking

In a similar vein, researchers reported in 2012 that people of higher social class are more likely to engage in unethical behaviors, such as taking candy meant for children, lying at work and cheating during games. Earlier this year, that study earned the authors an Ig Nobel Prize, a spoof award designed to “honor achievements so surprising that they make people laugh, then think.”

Next, the team turned to computer simulations using digital twins of each participant. They observed rule-breaking dynamics in groups of 100 digital twins at a time and found that occasionally, the few extreme deviants could turn the entire group into rule-breakers.

“Sometimes people do things in groups that they would never dream of doing alone,” Jens Krause, a behavioral ecologist at the Humboldt University of Berlin and the Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries, said a statement in 2022, after he and his colleagues had published a review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences on group rule-breaking. Krause did not participate in the new work.

Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who also wasn’t involved in the work, tells Science News’ Sujata Gupta that while the new study sheds light on human behavior without the pressure of consequences, it’s not a realistic imitation of the world. His research indicates that one should account for societal pressures like punishments and social norms to really comprehend social contagion and the rise of mobs.

articles.title: Shamonda Virus Infected and Killed a Person for the First Time. Here's What to Know About the Pathogen Usually Found in Livestock

paras.en: The first known human case of the Shamonda virus was reported by French authorities this month. The patient, a man in his 60s who had leukemia, died on October 9, just 16 days after showing neurological symptoms, including blindness and confusion.
The incident was described in a report released on October 22 in the journal Eurosurveillance.

In a statement translated by Smithsonian magazine, French health officials called it an exceptional case in a severely immunocompromised patient. They stressed that there is no risk to the public based on what is known about the Shamonda virus, which typically infects livestock. However, the fact that a human was infected suggests that scientists still have a lot to learn about the disease and how it affects the body.

Shamonda virus belongs to a family of viruses called orthobunyaviruses, and it’s primarily transmitted through tiny flies called midges, says Krispin Hajkowicz, an infectious-disease researcher at the University of Queensland in Australia, to Nature’s Rachel Fieldhouse. The pathogen commonly affects cattle, though infections have also been detected in sheep, horses, goats and alpacas.

The virus was first detected in cows in Nigeria in 1965, and since then has been detected in other parts of Africa and in Japan. The virus was found in Europe for the first time this past summer, when officials reported cases in German and Swiss cattle, per the World Health Organization. It rapidly made its way through dairy cows and horses in Western Europe, including Austria, Belgium and France.

Symptoms in animals include fever, diarrhea and reduced milk production. In more serious cases, it can also cause reproduction issues, like stillbirths and fetal malformations. Neurological conditions have also been reported in some horses, according to the World Organization for Animal Health, although this symptom is rare.
There are currently no treatments or vaccines for Shamonda virus.

Roughly six in ten known infectious diseases in humans can be spread from animals, and three in four new or emerging infectious diseases that affect people come in animals, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still aren’t sure. The patient lived in a rural area about an hour from Lyon, a city in eastern France, a region where Shamonda had been detected in cattle. Officials suspect that the deceased individual was bitten by a midge carrying the virus.

However, these insects typically don’t feed on animals, says Jean-Luc Guérin, a researcher at the National Veterinary School of Toulouse in France and co-author of the report, to Kai Kupferschmidt at Science. That’s why entomologists are trying to determine whether the disease can also spread via mosquitoes.
The risk to the public is low, as the patient in this case was already severely immunocompromised. There is currently no evidence that the virus can spread person-to-person.

John Drake, an infectious-disease researcher at the University of Georgia, writes in Forbes that he would only become worried if one of three things happened: a second human case with no shared exposure, a serious illness in someone with an intact immune system, or genomic evidence that the virus swapped genes with a better-adapted relative.

“Until one of them appears, Shamonda is a cattle virus spreading across Europe that is very probably linked to the death of one critically ill person,” he adds. “What is needed is surveillance: testing the sick, sequencing the strange case, watching the herds and the people among them. This death is a personal tragedy and an interesting case for science, but not a threat to public health.”

articles.title: A Fire Ravaged the 'Eagle's Nest,' an Alpine Retreat Built for Top Nazis. What Happens Next?

paras.en: Since the end of World War II, the Eagle’s Nest, a mountaintop retreat in the Bavarian Alps built for high-ranking Nazi officials, was preserved as a reminder of the “the insanity of the regime.” On Friday night, the building was almost entirely consumed by an inferno that authorities believe was an arson attack. The police have arrested a 33-year-old suspect who is currently in custody at a psychiatric hospital, according to a statement.

The first alarm sounded around 9:15 p.m. local time. By around 9:50 p.m., when emergency crews made it up the peak’s narrow, winding roads and tunnels, the building was already completely engulfed in flames.

Roughly 200 emergency personnel from six municipalities fought through the night to put out the fire. Containing the blaze proved nearly impossible. Firefighters struggled against fierce wind and rain that soon turned into the season’s first snowfall. Police spokesperson Lisa Maier said that the site’s high altitude of about 6,000 feet meant that crews had to wear “heavy breathing apparatus,” reports the Guardian’s Donna Ferguson.

Though smoke continued to rise from the charred remains of the building the following morning, officials confirmed that no one was inside during the fire, and no injuries were reported. The building—which hosts a restaurant, beer garden and exhibit on the site’s history—had already closed for the evening.

Authorities are offering a grim assessment for the future of the site, which, until recently, was one of few undamaged structures from the Nazi era. A police spokesperson told the German newspaper Bild that the site had suffered extensive damage and that the “house is unlikely to be saved,” per the Guardian.

Completed in 1938 and formally inaugurated on Adolf Hitler’s 50th birthday in 1939, the Eagle’s Nest, or the Kehlsteinhaus in German, was part of the Obersalzberg mountain retreat, an idyllic Nazi power center that also hosted the Berghof, Hitler’s alpine residence.

Reaching the Eagle’s Nest was an engineering feat. Visitors both past and present traveled along a road carved into the mountainside, entered an underground tunnel and rode a 407-foot-tall elevator to the guesthouse.
While other buildings at Obersalzberg were bombed by the Allies in 1945 and Hitler’s Berghof was demolished in 1952, the Eagle’s Nest survived and became a site of both remembrance and tourism.
The Eagle’s Nest was captured in 1945 by American troops, some of whom carved their names into the red marble fireplace, a gift from Italian dictator Benito Mussolini to Hitler.

Investigators are examining whether the suspected arson attack was motivated by site’s infamous past. The current suspect, whom first responders caught riding down the mountain road on a motorcycle, has ties to the local area and appears to have worked alone, reports Geir Moulson of the Associated Press (AP).

The blaze has reignited difficult questions regarding the future of the mountaintop site. Bavaria’s interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, pledged that the state, which owns the building, would consult with historians, local authorities and preservationists to determine the next steps.

“We’re not going to leave a ruin there,” he told reporters in the nearby town of Berchtesgaden, according to the AP. “I think we will be able to find a sensible solution … It is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance.”

articles.title: Best Dyson Vacuum Deals for Dyson Week 2026
articles.author: Nena Farrell

paras.en: Prime Day may be over, but there are still big sale events between now and Black Friday. Case in point: Dyson Week, where you can find several Dyson technology devices (vacuums! hair tools! massive air purifiers!) for a discounted price that you'd usually have to wait for a big sale holiday for. If you're in the market for a new Dyson vacuum, one of the best deals is on Dyson's newest, most powerful cordless vacuum: the Dyson V16 Piston Animal. articles.title: Why Anthropic’s IPO Prospectus Is Missing So Many Key Figures
articles.author: Lauren Goode, Caroline Haskins, Kate Taylor

paras.en: Anthropic filed its hotly anticipated IPO prospectus on Monday, spelling out parts of the company’s business, strategy, and risk profile ahead of its public debut. Though the filing, known as an S-1, is several hundred pages long, it has some notable omissions—namely, certain financial figures.

“Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $_____ for the three months ended September 30, 2026,” reads the first of dozens of such examples.

It’s relatively common for companies to redact certain information in their S-1 filings, and Securities and Exchange Commission rules allow for a certain degree of leniency around the practice, particularly when it comes to information considered “confidential.”

Still, it’s helpful to know what, exactly, these companies decide to leave out. In Anthropic’s case, the missing details largely revolve around financials for its most recent quarter, which concluded at the end of September, and lease agreements tied to its compute investments. While experts expect many details to be disclosed before Anthropic goes public, their current absence may hint at the uncertainties of investing in artificial intelligence, as companies work to secure sufficient compute.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

Michael Dambra, an accounting and law professor at the University at Buffalo School of Management, tells WIRED that there are “practical reasons” for Anthropic’s third-quarter numbers to be absent: September 30 was only a few weeks ago, and “closing the books for a company of this size takes time.”

Companies can also be liable for misstatements in their registration statements, “so there is a strong incentive not to publish numbers before they have been fully vetted,” Dambra says. SEC rules require that “Anthropic would need to update the filing with third-quarter financials” if the company goes public any later than about mid-November, he says.

As for data center lease agreements, Erica Neuman, an accounting professor at Youngstown State University, says it’s “not unusual” for companies to redact confidential details from “contract exhibits,” which could include lease terms.

However, Neuman adds that it’s worth scrutinizing whether Anthropic’s redactions would prevent, or make it more difficult, for investors to analyze Anthropic’s financial obligations and whether they may impact the company’s cash flow.

Many of Anthropic’s financial obligations relate to compute, which is the “most significant operating cost in our business,” according to the S-1. It’s also a business risk for the company, and it’s laid out both in terms of undersupply and overinvestment. (Parts of the AI industry have been warning that chip constraints could slow the progress of AI.)

Anthropic’s prospectus puts more emphasis on the risks of overinvestment, stating that the company needs to make forward investments in compute resources that will seem “irresponsibly large” at first glance.

Chips, Anthropic explains, are approached as a “single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners,” including Amazon, Google, Nvidia, and AMD. The company notes that it has entered into contracts “with an aggregate committed spend of more than $____, substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.” Some of these contracts are set to be completed before December 2030, while others may extend through 2045.

Though the prospectus touches on Anthropic’s compute uncertainties due to factors like limited land and power resources, Patrick Moorhead, CEO and chief analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, believes investors are owed more detail.

“It’s about characterizing the odds and impact individually across each of the areas. Anthropic owes investors more information, such as a probability of these individual issues, characterizing the percentage chance and the degree of the impact,” he tells WIRED. “Not ‘could materially impact.’”

Anthropic does provide some eye-catching estimates in footnotes. Since December 31, 2025, it has started or amended “compute and infrastructure” leases with “future minimum payment obligations” worth approximately $417 billion in aggregate. Since June 30, it has added an additional $245 billion to its future payment obligations, all related to infrastructure agreements. It also expanded “certain existing commercial agreements” that it caveats “have not yet been finalized,” for an additional $125 billion to $150 billion.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Include “short term” agreements with “minimum non-cancelable payments,” Anthropic says, and that’s another $21 billion. In total, it will owe, at minimum, an estimated $808 billion if it follows through on all of this.

Ben Bajarin, chief executive and a principal analyst at Creative Strategies who tracks the chip industry, says that this is likely just the first draft of Anthropic’s prospectus, and he expects a lot of gaps to be filled in an updated version.

Despite how common S-1 redactions are, Dambra describes them as “controversial.” While companies may argue that they’re “protecting proprietary information,” Dambra says that skeptics accuse them of using redactions “opportunistically” in order to “avoid disclosing politically or socially sensitive information.”

However, Dambra argues that redacting information may come at a cost. He notes that companies with redactions in their S-1s were also more likely to “underprice” their shares at the initial public offering.

When companies redact information in their S-1, Dambra says, they typically understand that they’ve created an “information gap” between them and outside investors. Understanding that investors will treat this gap with “suspicion,” companies may feel inclined to “entice” them to participate in the IPO by setting a lower starting price.

It’s unclear what Anthropic’s opening price may end up being or how investors may be interpreting the redactions in the company’s S-1. But according to Bajarin, the whole AI industry is one form of “blank” or another when it comes to crunching the numbers based on access to chips and infrastructure right now. So, yes, it’s all a risk.
“All of this,” he says, “just shows how absurdly early we are in enterprise adoption of an AI market that will be more than $3 trillion yearly and likely growing.”

articles.title: Grok Says Its AI-Generated Version of ‘The Odyssey’ Is ‘Not Historically Accurate’
articles.author: Miles Klee

paras.en: You don’t hear the defenders of so-called Western civilization talk much about The Odyssey these days.

Maybe that’s because their rabid denunciations of Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of Homer’s epic were buried in an avalanche of money. The July blockbuster has grossed nearly $1.8 billion worldwide, silencing the right-wingers who predicted a massive flop due to diverse casting and deviations from the source material.

Perhaps the loudest of these preemptive critics was Elon Musk. The world’s richest man spared no vitriol for what he considered a desecration of the ancient Greek narrative; four days after its release, he vowed to produce a superior version. “Before this year ends,” Musk wrote on X, “Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer.”

A little more than three months later—long after the discourse moved on—the public finally has a first glimpse of what we might call the Grodyssey, an Odyssey rendered through prompts fed into xAI’s video and image generation model. Rather than a “full-length movie,” it’s a seven-minute “episode” of an apparently ongoing series, depicting how Odysseus, king of Ithaca, resists a call to war against Troy but is ultimately compelled by an oath of loyalty to sail there with his army.

“Odyssey with Grok Imagine,” Musk announced Friday on X when sharing the clip, produced by AI entertainment company Wonder Studios X. The subdued post received just 18,000 likes, notably less engagement than other recent posts in which Musk cast doubt on the results of Brazil’s elections, complained about pronouns, and disparaged “legacy news.”

Grok’s introductory episode bears many hallmarks of AI slop. The movements of faces don’t match the dialog, which is further undercut by stilted and unnatural delivery. Besides Odysseus, none of the principal characters are introduced by name, and the pacing issues are laughable: The Ithacans arrive on the shores of Troy immediately after leaving their homeland, for example. Even the blue checks on X were harsh in their assessment. “Someone actually watched this and still decided to post it?” wrote one user. “Fire that person.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But Musk’s stated goal wasn’t to deliver a better-looking or more narratively cohesive version of The Odyssey. He and his culture war comrades dubiously claimed that they were against Nolan’s casting of Black and trans actors, the Americanized English spoken by the characters they played, and various designs of ships and armor in the film because they were “historically inaccurate.” Hence Musk’s guarantee of a “historically accurate” corrective.

So, did Grok Imagine succeed on that front? Asking Grok for a self-evaluation yields an interesting answer. “No,” the chatbot says when queried about whether this Odyssey snippet is historically accurate. “Grok Imagine’s Episode 1 (and the broader promised series) is an adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey, not a historically accurate reconstruction of real events.”

The AI model further notes that the characters have no basis in the historical record, and that the poem is dominated by “myth” and “invention” rather than confirmed events. “Homeric society mixes possible Bronze Age elements (palace-centered kingdoms, certain warrior practices) with later Iron Age features,” it also states. “Many details are anachronistic or literary.”

In laying out the reasons that the episode “does not meet a strict historical standard,” Grok points out that the characters speak modern English with British accents, “not Homeric Greek or any reconstructed Bronze Age language.” Visually, it says, the production reflects “modern cinematic tropes and AI training data,” not “primary archaeological evidence.” (The bot cites the appearance of cavalry in a battle scene as an error when compared with standard reconstructions of the period.) Grok concludes that “the Odyssey itself is not a historical document, and the production makes no serious attempt at archaeological or linguistic fidelity beyond a general ‘ancient Greek epic’ aesthetic.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Of course, the creative license that comes with adapting a millennia-old legend swarming with gods, witches, magic, and monsters was understood by just about everyone but Musk and a handful of cranks insisting that Nolan had contradicted some fundamentally true account of heroic adventure. Even Grok can tell you that its master’s fit of pique led him to promise the impossible—as he so often does.

articles.title: Tennessee inmate serving life sentence for murder escapes prison

paras.en: Oct. 26 (UPI) -- A state inmate serving a life sentence for murder escaped from a Tennessee prison over the weekend, prison authorities said Monday, as they asked the public for help in locating Jacob Allen Morley.
The 28-year-old escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville in northwestern Tennessee late Sunday night, the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement.
Prison officials said staff at the facility confirmed he was unaccounted for at 11:30 p.m. CDT Sunday, prompting an emergency count and search of the prison.
A review of security footage confirmed that Morley had breached the perimeter fence and exited the facility in his prison uniform, officials said, without providing specifics of the escape.

The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation later Monday said video obtained amid the search for Morley showed he had stolen a white pickup truck marked "Lindamood Planting Company" in Lake County, seemingly from a worksite at 1 a.m.
"Residents are urged to check home security systems, including doorbell cameras and trail cameras, for any sightings of Morley or the stolen truck," the TBI said in a statement.
TBI said Morley has been added to its Most Wanted list. A reward of up to $2,500 was being offered for information leading to the escaped convict's arrest, it added.
Morley is described as 5 feet, 11 inches tall and weighing approximately 240 pounds. He has brown hair and green eyes.
He was convicted and sentenced to life in prison in 2025 for murdering co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022.
According to the Carter County Sheriff's Office, Birchfield was reported missing by a family member on Feb. 23, 2022, after last being seen with Morley two days earlier.
Investigators determined a violent crime had occurred at Birchfield's residence and pursued Morley into North Carolina, where he was arrested in early March.
Authorities then found Birchfield's body during a search of Morley's residence.

articles.title: Brewers bombard Rays with 8-run inning to take 3-0 World Series lead

paras.en: Oct. 26 (UPI) -- Milwaukee Brewers batters were bloodthirsty piranhas, feasting on Tampa Bay Rays pitches for a World Series record eight two-out runs in the fifth inning of a Game 3 blowout Monday in St. Petersburg, Fla.
With the 10-1 victory, the Brewers moved within one win of their first title. They also could become the first team in MLB history to sweep their final two best-of-seven series en route to a crown.

The Rays, who will host Game 4 on Tuesday at Tropicana Field, were outhit 16 to 3 in the lopsided loss. Left fielder Jackson Chourio went 4 for 5, with two runs scored and an RBI for the Brewers, who reached their impressive run total without the assistance of a home run.
"We're gonna enjoy tonight," Brewers starter Robert Gasser, who allowed one hit over six shutout innings, said on the Fox broadcast. "It was a great team win, but we've got work to do.
"There is still one more game for us to win. I know everybody is eager to do it. We are going to show up tomorrow read to go."
The Brewers offense gave Gasser run support with back-to-back RBI singles from designated hitter Christian Yelich and catcher William Contreras in the third.
They unloaded on Rays starter Freddy Peralta with their record onslaught two innings later. A dozen Brewers batters came to the plate in the frame.

Second baseman Brice Turang plated Chourio and Yelich with an RBI single for the first runs of the inning. Center fielder Garrett Mitchell, shortstop Cooper Pratt, right fielder Sal Frelick, third baseman David Hamilton and Chourio proceeded to drive in additional runs over the next five consecutive at-bats.

Peralta allowed seven hits and five runs over 4 2/3 innings. The Rays scored their lone run off an RBI double from designated hitter Yandy Diaz in the bottom of the ninth. Diaz, who went 2 for 4, was the only Rays hitter to reach base more than once.
Turang went 3 for 4 with two RBIs and a run scored. Yelich went 2 for 3 with an RBI, run scored and a walk.
Chourio, who collected eight hits through three World Series games, became the youngest player (22) to log four hits in a World Series game since 1946 with Monday's performance.
"I love the game," Chourio said. "I love to play the game. I owe a lot to my family. ... My dad showed me how to play the game the right way."
First pitch for Game 4 is set for 8 p.m. EDT Tuesday in St. Petersburg. Game 5, if necessary, is set for the same time Wednesday at Tropicana Field.

articles.title: Justice Department charges James Comey a third time

paras.en: Oct. 26 (UPI) -- The U.S. Justice Department has charged former FBI Director James Comey with federal crimes for a third time, saying he allegedly leaked a national security document.

The charges were unsealed Monday, only hours after a federal judge ruled that the department unlawfully fired Comey's daughter, Maurene Comey, last year from her position as an assistant U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.

James Comey was charged through a criminal information rather than a grand jury indictment, in an effort by federal prosecutors to toll the statute of limitations. His defense attorneys filed a motion to dismiss the charges against him last week.

In a video statement published to his Substack, Comey rejected the charges, saying, "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice justice -- one that we cannot become numb to."

Comey said nothing has changed with him since the last time he was charged by the Justice Department: "I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."

In this case, the former FBI director is charged with knowingly communicating information related to national defense to someone not entitled to receive the information. He is also charged with conspiring to violate the law. The incident allegedly happened in October 2016.

In the charging document, known as criminal information, filed Oct. 5 in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., federal prosecutors alleged that Comey, "through one or more co-conspirators," directed an unnamed person to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication.

The case centers on an Oct. 5, 2016, article by The New York Times, according to a statement from Comey's attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, who said it was investigated by two different teams of prosecutors during President Donald Trump's first administration and both teams determined against bringing charges against anyone.

"Now, 10 years after the article was published, the government filed an 'information' against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury," he said, adding that they are grateful the matter has been unsealed and made public.
"Mr. Comey will fight these charges vigorously and in the open."

The Trump administration has targeted Comey, a former Republican, multiple times since Trump abruptly fired him in May 2017. As FBI director, Comey oversaw the start in March 2017 of an inquiry into Russian interference in the 2016 election.

In April, a federal grand jury in North Carolina indicted Comey on charges related to his posting on social media a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to form the numbers "86 47." The Justice Department said the "86" post -- often used in restaurants to indicate that a menu item is no longer available -- was interpreted by prosecutors as a threat against Trump, the 47th president.
Comey's attorneys have sought the dismissal of that case.
The first Justice Department charges against Comey -- for alleged false testimony to the U.S. Senate -- were dismissed in November 2025.

At the time, Comey posted a video on social media saying, "A message has to be sent that the president of the United States cannot use the Department of Justice to target his political enemies. I don't care what your politics are, you have to see that as fundamentally un-American and a threat to the rule of law that keeps all of us free."
"I know that Donald Trump will probably come after me again," he said, "and my attitude is going to be the same. I'm innocent, I am not afraid, and I believe in an independent federal judiciary."
Asked by reporters about the charges against Comey late Monday, Trump said that "I don't know too much about it. I just heard about it."
"I think he's a dirty cop, James Comey, but I know nothing about it," he said.

Since returning to office, Trump has employed the power of the executive office to impose what critics have characterized as punitive measures against his perceived political opponents, including law firms linked to his critics, prosecutors who brought cases against him between his first and second terms and elected officials such as Rep. Jason Crow and Sen. Adam Schiff and New York Attorney General Letitia James.

articles.title: Jay-Z to Headline 2027 Super Bowl Halftime Show: ‘GOAT’s Out of the Bag’
articles.author: Katie Atkinson

paras.en: From halftime producer to headliner: Jay-Z is set to headline the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show.

The news was announced during Monday Night Football (Oct. 26) after ESPN teased a “special announcement” heading into halftime. A teaser soundtracked by “Public Service Announcement (Interlude),” off 2003’s The Black Album, plays across a black-and-white video of Jay-Z in stadium seats, kicking off with the famous line: “Allow me to reintroduce myself, my name HOV — H to the O-V.” The tease was posted to social media after.

The video includes the caption “GOAT’s out of the bag” since this became an open secret when it was reported first by Puck that Jay-Z — who’s been producing the halftime show alongside Roc Nation since 2020 — had given himself the nod to headline the 2027 Super Bowl set.

In fact, the rapper was expected to announce the news over the weekend, when he played a pair of shows at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, which will host the 2027 Super Bowl, on Friday and Saturday. Those shows came and went without an announcement, as did a full day of NFL games on Sunday, but now the news is official.

Given the Feb. 14 date of next year’s Super Bowl, fans are hopeful that Jay might be joined by his superstar wife Beyoncé for an unconventional Valentine’s Day celebration on the football field, among other possible special guests the rapper has collaborated with over the years.

Jay-Z, under his birth name Shawn Carter, has received six consecutive Primetime Emmy nominations as an executive producer of the Super Bowl halftime show, in the category of outstanding variety special (live). He won for two of those shows — the all-star hip-hop show in 2022 starring Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg, Mary J. Blige, Eminem, Kendrick Lamar and 50 Cent, and this year’s Latin spectacular starring Bad Bunny. Carter won a third Primetime Emmy in 2023 for co-directing the halftime show starring Rihanna, in the category of outstanding directing for a variety special.

paras.en: Last year’s Super Bowl halftime show — presented by Apple Music — was headlined by Bad Bunny, with special appearances from Lady Gaga and Ricky Martin, as well as celebrities hanging out in his on-field casita.

articles.title: Macklemore, Hozier and Kneecap Play Sold-Out Free Palestine Benefit Concert in Dublin
articles.author: Jessica Lynch

paras.en: Macklemore kicked off his Free Palestine benefit concert series in Dublin on Monday night (Oct. 26), bringing out Hozier, Kneecap and a stacked bill of guests at a sold-out 3Arena.

Joining the Seattle rapper onstage were Irish folk band Beoga, singer-songwriter Lina Makoul, M1 of Dead Prez and DJ Habibeats. Game of Thrones actor Liam Cunningham, activist and psychotherapist Nadia Greenspan and artist and organizer Samir Eskanda spoke as special guests, while Mark Ruffalo, The Strokes frontman Julian Casablancas, Cynthia Nixon, Ilana Glazer and Natasha Rothwell made remote appearances.

The three-city run is raising money for organizations that provide humanitarian relief, medical care, education and advocacy for Palestinians, according to organizers. When the series was announced in September, Live Nation named beneficiaries including Anera, Medical Aid for Palestinians, the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, Jewish Voice for Peace and UNRWA USA.

The shows grew out of Macklemore’s abrupt exit from the North American leg of Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour in September. During a stop at MetLife Stadium, he told the crowd “Free Palestine” and voiced support for people in Gaza and the West Bank. Macklemore later said New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft pushed for his removal, and Kraft confirmed he had barred the rapper from Gillette Stadium, citing those comments and what he called “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery.” Sheeran said the decision was made by his promoter, not him.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The fallout spread quickly. Several support acts quit the tour in response, among them Beoga, who had been performing with Sheeran every night before landing a spot on Monday’s Dublin bill. Macklemore has also pledged his $1 million in net earnings from the tour to Palestinian aid groups.

Dublin came just days after Macklemore played his first show since leaving the tour, a 17-song set at Colorado’s Red Rocks Amphitheatre on Oct. 22, where he again called for a “free Palestine” and spoke about Sudan, Congo, Lebanon, Haiti and people affected by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Macklemore has topped the Billboard Hot 100 twice, both alongside Ryan Lewis in 2013 with “Thrift Shop” and “Can’t Hold Us.”
The series moves to Paris’ Accor Arena on Thursday (Oct. 29) and wraps at London’s OVO Arena Wembley on Friday (Oct. 30). All three dates are sold out.

articles.title: Taylor Swift Says Nashville Songwriters ‘Raised Me’ During Hall of Fame Induction
articles.author: Jessica Lynch

paras.en: Taylor Swift was inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame on Monday night (Oct. 26), using her acceptance speech to revisit the Music Row writing rooms, publishers and collaborators who shaped her earliest years as a songwriter.

Brad Paisley inducted the 14-time Grammy winner at the organization’s 56th annual gala at Nashville’s Music City Center, prompting an opening joke about a tour prank that apparently still hadn’t been forgotten.
“I’m really surprised to see you here, actually, because we’ve been estranged since 2007,” Swift joked.

The singer-songwriter recalled Paisley filling her tour bus with thousands of live crickets during their time on the road together. “For months, I couldn’t sleep. Just chirp, chirp, chirp, chirp all night,” she remembered, before deciding his introduction had been good enough to let “bygones be bygones.”
From there, Swift broke the Hall of Fame honor down into three words: Nashville, songwriters and fame.
“I knew from the time I wrote my first song that even if it couldn’t be my career, it would be my passion,” she told the room. “It would be what I centered my entire life around.”
Nashville, meanwhile, was “the place that I went to in my middle school daydreams” — somewhere the young songwriter imagined all of the lessons and wisdom she wanted to acquire existed in one place.
“Fame, you know, that’s sort of a byproduct of my love for music,” the pop superstar explained. “It’s kind of like songwriter plus Nashville equals fame.”

With that success came what she described as “daily random doses of chaos.” When life starts to feel strange, Swift returns mentally to her earliest memories of arriving in Nashville, signing a publishing deal at 14 and writing songs every day.
“I was like a sponge,” she joked. “And I had really curly hair and it was yellow, so I kind of looked like a sponge too.”
Those formative years taught her that songwriting was a craft built through repetition.
“I think you truly learn a craft when you do it over and over and over,” the songwriter reflected. “And that is what the magnificent songwriters that work in this amazing town do.”
“There is no music community like this music community,” she added. “I know, I checked all the communities.”

Swift also credited Nashville’s writing community with teaching her some of the less glamorous realities of collaboration: how to push through creative blocks, which ideas are worth fighting for and when to let something go.
“I learned how to accommodate when your co-writer has a hangover, or when they’re going to need to talk about their divorce for a really long time before we write anything,” she joked.
Those writers, the newly inducted Hall of Famer explained, “in a lot of ways, raised me and guided me through my formative years.”
One memory she revisited in detail dates back to December 2005.

Her mother would pick her up from Hendersonville High School and drive her to Jody Williams Music, an independent publisher housed in a small Craftsman-style home. At the front desk was Katherine — whose boyfriend at the time, Swift revealed to the room, was Eric Church.
“Things have gone great for them,” she joked. “They’ve got a couple kids, married like 20 years now. His full name is Eric Church, just for clarity.”
From there, the then-teenage songwriter would run upstairs to a red-painted room to work with Liz Rose.
“I’d be like, ‘Liz, this happened in school today,’” Swift recalled. “And she’d get her notebook, and we’d just write so fast.”
After those sessions, she would head into a garden shed behind the building, where demo producer Nathan Chapman recorded her songs and played every instrument.
“He interpreted my music so intuitively that later on I would fight for him to produce my entire first album,” she recalled. “And it was our first album, both of us.”
Her self-titled debut celebrated its 20th anniversary on Oct. 24, just two days before Monday’s induction.
The “Love Story” singer also looked back on writing at Nashville’s Sony Fire Hall, where she could hear other songwriters working through the walls.
“I just kind of liked to pretend that I was in the real building,” she told the audience.
Looking back across the two decades that followed, Swift credited the foundation she built in Nashville with giving her the freedom to move between genres, collaborators and creative approaches.

“The only reason that I’ve been able to have that kind of dexterity in my creative process is because of the fundamentals and the foundation that I learned here in Nashville,” she said. “And I never forget that for a single second.”
“I’m so incredibly honored to be inducted into this sacred club, especially at this point in my life,” the newly minted Hall of Famer continued. “It’s not lost on me how crazy this is.”
She closed by describing Nashville as the place that “honed and polished” the part of herself she is most proud of.
“It just feels like one of those amazing Nashville moments I’m going to revisit on a rainy day,” Swift concluded.

Taylor Swift was inducted alongside Lyle Lovett, Shawn Camp, Lee Thomas Miller, Bruce Channel and the late J.I. Allison. Lainey Wilson performed a bluegrass rendition of “Love Story,” which peaked at No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100, while George Strait received the Career Maker Award.

articles.title: Tokyo: Competition Jury Discusses Event’s ‘A-List’ Status, Fighting Over Favorite Films
articles.author: Abid Rahman

paras.en: A lively discussion about the global standing of the Tokyo International Film Festival — and whether such considerations even matter — was the highlight of a rather genteel competition jury press conference on Tuesday.

The 2026 Tokyo competition jury is headed by Dutch-Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer (Bad Boy Bubby, Charlie’s Country, Ten Canoes and The Tracker), and he was joined on stage by competition jury members: French film colorist and producer Yov Moor; leading South Korean producer Oh Jungwan; veteran Japanese actress Makiko Watanabe; and Taiwanese-American producer Alex C. Lo.

In stark contrast to many recent pressers at the major European and American film festivals, the Tokyo jury conversation was largely politics free, though the event kicked off with an amusingly blunt answer from De Heer as to why there aren’t more Australian and Japanese co-productions.

De Heer was asked about the conspicuous lack of co-productions between Australia and Japan, despite both countries having strong state backing to film production. “It makes no sense for a Japanese film to shoot in Australia, or it makes no sense for an Australian film to shoot in Japan,” said De Heer. “Europe is very good at doing co-productions strictly on a financial basis, really. Australia is not so good at that. The sort of co-productions that work out of Australia are ones that are natural—that have a natural story where some things need to be shot in Japan, some things need to be shot in Australia. Those will always be possible if the scripts come and if they’re right.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: After the jury members spoke about their great honor at being invited to oversee this year’s competition, the conversation became a touch more animated when they were asked about the standing of Tokyo Film Festival, as compared to other international festivals, and specifically about Tokyo’s recent inclusion as an “A-list” event by the International Federation of Film Producers Associations (FIAPF).

“I think Tokyo was… has always been considered one of those festivals by most people who attend festivals,” said De Heer. “Tokyo was effectively an ‘A’ festival. And so in that sense, I don’t think it makes a lot of difference. This sort of categorization seems to be becoming more important in terms of the quality of films available to that festival, and so in that sense it may help that it is officially now again an ‘A’, but I don’t think it changes the festival so much.”

“I think Rolf’s answer is… is enough for… is not enough for you?” said Oh to laughter in the room. “Actually, I don’t know about that. I’m not a film festival person, so I don’t know what is A-list or not. Probably A-list means good! But as an audience, we’re not going to the festival because of their A-list or not. We just go to watch film and enjoy the festival feeling.”
Asked whether the tier system was somewhat redundant nowadays, De Heer replied cryptically, “It matters a great deal to some people, and not at all to others. And that is as it should be.”

Later in the discussion, Lo returned to the status of Tokyo, suggesting the festival’s reputation was built upon two key operational traits: world-leading festival hospitality and an exceptionally attentive, intellectually curious audience that respects original storytelling.

Looking ahead to the competition for the Tokyo Grand Prix, the jury also discussed how they would handle disagreements over the 15 films selected to compete. “It depends entirely on the very specific situation—how much disagreement, how divided is the jury,” said De Heer. “I don’t think there is an answer to that until we get to that point. As far as I understand it, I’m with four other very reasonable people, and I’m sure we can find a way through so that we don’t end up with some sort of lesser compromise film, but a really interesting film that maybe some of us don’t like.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Oh added jokingly that she was ready to fight De Heer over the selection. “Sometimes you want to fight for the film,” she added. “I had an experience where I fought for 7 hours with another jury! Every other jury member hated me. [laughter] But we are grownups and there are so many good films, so we will find a good way to compromise. I hope I don’t fight with him for 7 hours this time!”

Elsewhere, Moor spoke of his delight at being invited to sit on the jury, especially given film colorists are often overlooked for such roles. “When I received the invitation I was very surprised, because [with] my job [as a colorist] it [is] quite rare to receive this kind of invitation. And for me… now I’m almost two years in Tokyo… for me it was a very great surprise, and also for people who do the same job as me, to be able to be a jury at a film festival.” Moor added, “For me, it’s like a little dream, and also maybe to try to show more of my job as a colorist—not only me, but people who do the same job as me.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: De Heer, in his taciturn manner, also spoke about his future plans. Asked about his next film, the director said, “I don’t know… I am in-between, and I’m trying to make decisions about what to do.” He added, “This is another good reason why I enjoy being here, because it is a punctuation point. It’s not a very good answer for you, but it is the answer.”

articles.title: Tokyo: TIFFCOM Market Chief On Riding the Japanese IP Wave as Entertainment Landscape Shifts Due to AI
articles.author: Gavin Blair

paras.en: As Tokyo International Film Festival has raised its game and its profile over recent years, its content market TIFFCOM has been carving out its own niche, bolstered by the attractiveness of Japanese IP.
On top of attracting more exhibitors and visitors, the market has expanded its seminar offerings, landing bigger industry names to speak at them.

In addition to the popularity of anime, the potential of manga and gameshow IP, and the success of Japan-related productions like Shōgun, interest in Japan itself is at an all-time high – nearly 43 million people visited last year. This concatenation of factors is delivering a boost to the fest and the market, acknowledges TIFFCOM managing director Kaori Ikeda.

“It definitely is…Tokyo is probably one of the most fascinating cities in the world, and Japan is enjoying a boom. So definitely this supports our activities, because we are dealing with culture,” Ikeda tells The Hollywood Reporter as she and the TIFFCOM team were putting the final touches to preparations a few days before the market opens.

Ikeda is in her third year as TIFFCOM managing director following a career with Japanese indie distributor Asmik Ace – where her acquisitions included Trainspotting and Dead Man Walking, “those kinds of good old ones” – a project with DreamWorks and five years at Japanese cable major J:COM.

Among the initiatives she points to is the relaunch last year of Tokyo Story Market, which focused on book adaptation with Japanese publishing companies, as Tokyo IP Market: Adaptation & Remake, with a broader remit, this year bringing in remake-rights holders including film companies such as Toei and Shochiku, and toy company Takara Tomy.

“This year Japan was the Country of Honour at the Cannes Marché du Film, which we collaborated with and took Tokyo IP Market there to introduce Japanese IP that could be adapted in various ways, into film, games or any other form,” says Ikeda, who emphasizes that it is being backed by major investment from the Japanese government and industry.

Ikeda hails the Cannes venture a success that is likely to happen again, saying it brought together international producers and Japanese rights holders, and that she would like to include some smaller publishers which have limited experience in the global marketplace.
TIFFCOM logged about 4,600 visitors and 300 exhibitors in 2025, up strongly from previous editions, and is on track to equal or exceed those figures this year.

In line with the remake and co-production themes, the ‘Unlocking the Global Potential of Japanese IP’ session will feature producer Shinzo Matsuhashi (Kokuhō, Kingdom), Steven Maeda (Netflix’s One Piece), and Amazon MGM Studios Japan head Buddy Marini.

“And this year we are adding AI as a keynote. We have invited the executives from AGBO, Chris Brearton and Dominic Hughes for the Keynote: Technology and Storytelling, which we are very thrilled with,” adds Ikeda.
The Association of Japanese Animations will again release its annual industry data at its TIFFCOM session, while TV stations will present case studies of overseas format sales.

Another success story that Ikeda points to is the Tokyo Gap-Financing Market, now in its seventh year of linking partially funded projects with production partners. Two now completed productions from last year will be screened in this edition of the festival’s Crosscut Asia+ section. Meanwhile, The Violinist, an animation which found an Italian partner at the 2023 event, took home the top award at Annecy this year, reports Ikeda proudly.

All the while, the industry is shifting as are viewing habits. Short dramas are winning over audiences – not least in Japan – streamers recently seen as saviors are cutting budgets and AI is disrupting.
“There are so many things happening in the market at the moment…So, we’re looking at how to be a better place for the industry to have business meetings and also to network,” adds Ikeda.
TIFFCOM runs Oct. 28 to 30 at the Tokyo Metropolitan Industrial Trade Center Hamamatsucho-kan.

articles.title: The ‘Sukiyaki’ Phenomenon: The Song Behind the Tokyo Film Festival’s Opening Film
articles.author: Gavin Blair

paras.en: Opening the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival is Sukiyaki, Takahisa Zeze’s drama charting the backstory of the 1960s song that became a global hit and a symbol of Japan’s recovery from postwar devastation and humiliation.

Centered on composer and jazz pianist Hachidai Nakamura (Junichi Okada), the film tells of his partnership with lyricist Rokusuke Ei (Tori Matsuzaka), and how singer Kyu Sakamoto (Taiga Nakano) turned their combination of a jaunty melody and plaintive lyrics into an unlikely global pop culture phenomenon. Though the tale behind the tune was ripe for onscreen telling, the song’s legacy is perhaps even more remarkable.

An ill-fated recital left Nakamura struggling with debt and addiction as rockabilly eclipsed jazz. He was save by forging an unlikely partnership with Ei, a radio writer who had never penned song lyrics, to write a rockabilly score for a 1959 movie from Toho (the company also distributing the 2026 film).

In 1961, Nakamura and Ei wrote “Ue o Muite Aruko“, which translates as ‘I look upwards as I walk,’ for which Nakamura incorporated traditional Japanese scales, jazz chords and U.S. pop influences. Ei’s melancholic lyrics were inspired by the failure of the mass Anpo protests to stop a Tokyo-Washington security treaty that maintained a huge American military presence in Japan, and the looking upwards in the song is to stop tears of sadness falling from his eyes.

Singer Sakamoto was brought in on short notice for its premiere at Tokyo’s Sankei Hall on July 21, 1961 – only given the sheet music two hours beforehand. Unrehearsed, Sakamoto went into a minor key on an ad lib, sang the 4-beat song as an 8-beat, and came in a beat late, mimicking Japanese balladeers he had grown up listening to. These quirks added further layers to the song’s distinctiveness.
Released as a single, it was the Music Life best domestic song from November 1961 to January 1962, selling 300,000 copies.

It found its way overseas via Louis Benjamin of British label Pye Records visiting Japan in 1962 and falling for its catchy melody. He gave it to Kenny Ball and his Jazzmen to record an instrumental version titled “Sukiyaki,” which made the British top ten in February 1963. One story is that Benjamin came up with the name after eating sukiyaki, a hotpot dish, in Tokyo, while another version has Ball picking one of the only Japanese words he knew because he figured the original title was too difficult for listeners.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: After a U.S. release of Ball’s version, and another instrumental cover by Billy Vaughn, failed to make waves, Capitol US decided to gamble on the original Japanese version — but with the “Sukiyaki” title. It hit record stores on May 3, 1963 and in June topped the Billboard Hot 100 for three weeks. This made Sakamoto the only Japanese artist to ever have a U.S. No.1, and the song the first from Asia to do so. It would not be until BTS’s “Dynamite” in 2020 that another Asian artist would repeat that feat.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The appeal of the infectious tune and Sakamoto’s whistling reached far beyond the U.S., with “Sukiyaki” topping rankings from Australia to Norway. The single eventually sold more than 13 million copies worldwide.

As the Japanese public began to realize people around the world were whistling along to a song in their native tongue, Toshiba capitalized and reissued the single. The 1963 cover added “Sukiyaki” to the title, rendered in the katakana syllabary for foreign words, along with the packaging legend: “global hit!”

Japan’s economy was by then registering double-digit growth as companies like Sony and Toyota were becoming global brands. The worldwide success of “Sukiyaki” was another source of pride for a national psyche still bruised by wartime defeat and occupation.

International cover versions of “Sukiyaki” then came thick and fast, with dozens in Chinese languages alone, as well as interpretations in Spanish, German and French. Scores of Japanese artists have also covered the song.

Among the U.S. fans of the 1963 release was a nine-year-old Janice-Marie Johnson, who later founded R&B and funk outfit A Taste of Honey. A few years after their No.1 hit Boogie Oogie Oogie, Johnson decided she wanted to do a version of “Sukiyaki” and contacted lyricist Ei in Japan, who provided her with a rough English translation. She worked these into her own take on the song, but faced stiff opposition from her label and producer, who were convinced R&B audiences had no interest in Japanese-sounding music. Johnson’s persistence was justified when their “Sukiyaki” topped the Billboard R&B chart and reached number three on the Hot 100 in 1981. The band appeared alongside Sakamoto on Japanese TV.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Johnson’s lyrics were used in hip-hop duo Doug E. Fresh & Slick Rick’s 1985 classic “La Di Da Di.”

On the evening of August 12, 1985 Sakamoto boarded Japan Air Lines flight 123 from Tokyo to Osaka. Twelve minutes after takeoff the Boeing 747 suffered catastrophic mechanical failure. The pilots managed to keep the plane in the air for around half an hour — enough time for many passengers to write messages to loved ones — before it crashed into a mountainside in central Japan, killing 520 of the 524 onboard, including Sakamoto. It remains the deadliest single-aircraft disaster in aviation history. Sakamoto’s song is played at the annual memorial service.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Sukiyaki” was revived as a symbol of melancholic hope in the wake of the 2011 earthquake, tsunami and nuclear disaster in Japan when it was sung by 71 celebrities in a television commercial. It was also featured in that year’s Ghibli movie From Up on Poppy Hill, leading to a reissue.
Tokyo Ska Paradise Orchestra played it at the closing ceremony of the pandemic-delayed Tokyo Olympics in August 2021.
Sukiyaki, the film, opens in Japan on Christmas Day, reuniting on screen the trio Sakamoto had said he wanted to bring back together just days before his death.

articles.title: Morningstar CEO Kunal Kapoor on making career choices that help you grow

paras.en: Why Kunal Kapoor turned down a better-paid job to join Morningstar
Kunal Kapoor faced a choice early in his career: accept a higher-paid job in banking or join a little-known investment research firm called Morningstar.

Despite encouragement from those closest to him to take the more secure option, Kapoor trusted his instincts and chose Morningstar. Nearly three decades later, he's still there — having risen through the ranks to become CEO.

In the latest episode of Executive Decisions, Kapoor tells CNBC's Steve Sedgwick why he believes it's important to find opportunities for personal growth, how his approach to leadership has evolved and what he learned from hiring mistakes earlier in his career.
He also discusses Morningstar's expansion into private markets, the challenges of leading through technological change and why AI is forcing businesses to rethink how they operate.

articles.title: Oil falls as renewed diplomatic efforts to end Mideast conflict ease supply concerns

paras.en: Oil prices fell Tuesday as renewed diplomatic efforts to end the U.S.-Iran war raise hopes of a de-escalation in the wider regional conflict that has seen Tehran-backed Houthis target Saudi Arabia.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery slipped 0.87% to $114.80 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for June declined 0.86% to $100.88 per barrel.
The pullback followed talks between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan and Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday, as they stepped up efforts to defuse tensions across the Middle East.

Riyadh said the discussions were aimed at keeping diplomatic channels open and preventing another escalation in hostilities. The four countries agreed to continue to engage to advance regional peace and security, according to Iranian state media.

The diplomatic push comes as U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with Fox News on Sunday that he was approaching a decision on whether to strike a deal with Iran or intensify military operations, suggesting that additional attacks remained an option.
Representatives from Qatar, which has helped mediate negotiations between Washington and Tehran, also traveled to the Iranian capital on Sunday, Reuters reported.
Prospects of a diplomatic breakthrough have helped temper fears of further disruptions to global energy supplies, putting downward pressure on crude prices.
Still, losses remained limited as the prospect of a lasting resolution appeared fragile, with Iran-backed Houthi militants continuing their attacks on Saudi Arabia over the weekend.
—CNBC's Justina Lee contributed to the report.

articles.title: HSBC announces share buyback of up to $1 billion as third-quarter profit meets estimates

paras.en: Europe's largest bank HSBC on Tuesday announced a share buyback of up to $1 billion and reported third-quarter pretax profit that largely met analysts' estimates.

Revenue at HSBC rose to $18.6 billion from $17.8 billion in the same period last year, while banking net interest income rose 6%, alongside the bank clocking higher fee income form its corporate and institutional banking and wealth business.
Here are HSBC's third -quarter results compared with the consensus estimates compiled by the bank.
- Pre-tax profit: $9.63 billion vs. $9.69 billion expected
- Revenue: $18.6 billion vs. $18.93 billion expected

The bank's third-quarter profit before tax increased 32% from a year earlier to $9.6 billion, also reflecting the absence of $1.4 billion in legal provisions recorded in the same period last year. Higher revenue and lower credit losses also supported earnings.
Shares in HSBC, which approved a third interim divided of 10 cents per share, fell 2.95% in Hong Kong following the release of its third-quarter earnings.
The bank's net interest income rose to $9.3 billion in the third quarter, supported by deposit growth and reinvestment of its "structural hedge at higher yields."

Meanwhile, operating expenses decreased 12% year on year to $8.8 billion, largely due to non-recurrence of legal provisions recorded a year earlier. Excluding notable items, expenses rose amid inflation and higher spending on technology.

Looking ahead, HSBC maintained its forecast for banking net interest income of at least $46 billion in 2026, while reiterating its target for return on average tangible equity — a metric for assessing profitability — of 17% or higher for 2026 through 2028, excluding notable items.
The bank also expects revenue to grow annually through 2028, targeting 5% growth that year compared with 2027, excluding notable items and on a constant currency basis.

HSBC said it remains on track to deliver operating expense growth of approximately 1% in 2026 on a target basis, although strong business performance could lead to additional performance-related pay and modestly higher cost growth.
The bank said it had bought back $1 billion in shares announced at its interim results, and expects to complete another $1 billion in buybacks before its full-year 2026 results.
HSBC is reportedly considering significant job cuts in its U.K. wealth management business, as part of a broader push to adopt artificial intelligence.

articles.title: The Trump administration is considering a ‘heat ray’ weapon for the border—here’s what to know

paras.en: The Pentagon has granted the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a controversial and little-used “heat ray” weapon at the U.S.-Mexico border, prompting questions over how safe it is and how it works.

The weapon is called the Active Denial System, and it is considered a nonlethal weapon: it causes pain but is not supposed to damage tissue. It works using millimeter waves, which—true to their name—have wavelengths between one and 10 millimeters. Millimeter waves are also used in full-body scanners, such as those in airports—but the military weapon puts out its 95-gigahertz waves at a higher intensity for just a few seconds at a time, says Kenneth Foster, a professor emeritus of bioengineering at the University of Pennsylvania.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This energy penetrates about 0.4 mm, the thickness of about four sheets of standard printer paper, of the skin, where it excites water molecules in cells and heats them up. The feeling is reportedly similar to standing in front of a hot oven. “It causes intense pain, but the exposure is not long enough to do damage,” Foster says.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

If the weapon is used at the border, it will mark one of the few uses of this technology ever since its development in the early 2000s, as CNN reported on Wednesday. According to the nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights (PHR), the system was used briefly in Afghanistan in 2010 but has not been employed in warfare since then. Prison officials in Los Angeles considered testing the device for riot control in 2010, yet pushback from civil rights groups and the Federal Communications Commission led to the program being scrapped.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “The weapon is politically toxic,” Foster says.

The system is bulky and temperamental; it doesn’t work well in rain, fog or mist because the moisture attenuates the heating effect on the targeted person. Foster suspects that the system’s cost, expense and bulk have a lot to do with why it hasn’t been used more; other nonlethal methods such as sound cannons are cheaper and more available, he says.

Persistent concerns about the safety of something that sounds suspiciously like a microwave oven are also a barrier. Microwaves, with their longer wavelengths, penetrate farther into skin and can cause more damage. Military testing suggests that exposure to millimeter-wave nonlethal weapons does not cause skin damage. Tests on volunteers in 2005 and 2006 did lead to a handful of people getting skin blisters and rashes, however. An incident in 2007 in which the weapon was set at the incorrect power and pulse duration led to one airman receiving second-degree blistering burns on 8 percent of his body. So it is possible that improper usage could cause injury.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “There is very, very little published on these weapons,” says Rohini Haar, an emergency physician at the University of California, Berkeley, School of Public Health and a medical adviser at PHR. Without published research, she says, there is little information on their safety in general or on potential differences in safety in real-world usage versus experimental or training exercises.
John Erath, Senior Policy Director for the Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation, a nonprofit, points out that testing such weapons in human trials for safety is “an ethical dead-end.”

PHR has also documented numerous cases of crowd-control weapons being used against people with no easy way to escape. Indiscriminate use of the system could cause injury not just from the heat itself but also from the reaction of those targeted, says Michael Crowley. He is a senior researcher at the U.K.-based nonprofit Omega Research Foundation, which tracks the use of military and police weapons and human rights abuses.

“Given its silent and invisible nature, the ‘pain ray’ makes avoidance of the weapon difficult, which could prevent people from dispersing safely, lead to panic-driven stampedes and consequent serious injuries,” Crowley says.

“Furthermore, those subsequently injured or crowd members who have existing mobility difficulties, including the elderly and very young, may not be able to leave the area and then be subject to repeated or prolonged exposure of this weapon, potentially leading to further intolerable pain and serious injuries,” he adds.

articles.title: Meet the original 'Ghost Busters'—the 17th-century scientists who investigated hauntings

paras.en: About 1671, parson Symonds, who officiated at Garsdon church in north Wiltshire in south west England, was riding home late one night when a specter leapt up behind him. The specter rode parallel to him until they came to the parsonage, where it jumped off. The apparition then turned to face Symonds, and “gap’d at him”. Symonds identified the ghost as that of John Estcourt, a gentleman who had died about two years earlier.

Halloween is all about witches and ghosts. In English scientific circles in the second half of the 17th century, there was a discussion about whether such things existed and how their existence could be proved.

The Royal Society, founded in 1660, was the country’s principal scientific institution. Joseph Glanvill, a Royal Society fellow, investigated spirits and witches. His Saducismus Triumphatus(1681) aimed to prove their existence by cataloguing cases in detail. He argued that denying them was to deny God’s existence.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Symonds’ haunting was recorded by that of another of the society’s fellows, John Aubrey, in a survey of Wiltshire’s natural world. Aubrey agreed with Glanvill that the supernatural deserved serious study and directed his readers to Saducismus, but he thought Glanvill somewhat gullible.
Aubrey was born in 1626 at Easton Piercy, a few miles from Garsdon. I have edited John Aubrey’s Natural History to mark his 400th anniversary.

This natural history of Wiltshire was begun in 1656 and was the first English county survey of nature to be attempted – although by the time he finished it, decades later, other surveys had already been published. It was an important scientific work, and in 1691, acknowledging that, the Royal Society had the Natural History copied and added to its library.

Its subject matter is highly idiosyncratic, and Aubrey sometimes goes off on tangents. He covers swan-sized dragons in north Africa in a chapter on birds and the existence of giants in a section called “Men and Women”. Almost at the end of the text is a chapter titled “Accidents” that records extraordinary events, including supernatural ones, like the haunting of Symonds.
Aubrey has long been seen as naive, partly because of Miscellanies (1696), the only book he published, which recorded tales of the unexplained. In the Natural History, he was clear:

Though I myselfe never saw any such things, yet I will not conclude that there is no truth at all in these reports. I believe that extraordinarily there have been such apparitions: but where one is true, a hundred are figments.

He also documented exposed frauds, such as Katherine Waldron, who pretended to be bewitched and endured pins being driven into her flesh to prove it. As the objective of natural history at this time was to gather evidence from which new scientific theories could be developed, Aubrey’s method in chronicling cases was entirely in keeping with the aims of scientific enterprise.

So, Aubrey was neither uncritical nor dismissive about Symonds’ story. Symonds was “a lusty strong fellow”, presumably not someone nervous or hysterical and prone to flights of imagination. His position as a churchman also gave authority to his testimony. Yet Aubrey noted a French saying that drunk men saw devils, a skeptical observation that cast doubt on the account. But he concluded with a strange detail: it was corroborated by the parson’s horse, “that trembled and sweat, when he came home and continued to do so the next day, and would not eat his oates”. The horse could not lie or get drunk; its fear, manifest in the trembling and sweat, was genuine.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Aubrey recorded another anecdote about a night ride. It concerned Sir Ralph Bankes’ valet:“a briske young fellow”, who, riding late over Badbury Warren, Dorset, discerned something that looked black, which, as he approached, became bigger.
Feare came upon him, and he protested his haire stood on end: but thought he, I have but a life to lose and I will see it, be it spirit or not.
The valet spurred his horse and came to the place, only to find the apparition was “a heap of horse dung”.

In Symonds’ haunting, the truth of the specter could not be tested; but witnesses were recorded, and their testimony weighed. In the valet’s case, the witness tested the truth of the ghost himself and found it was a pile of dung.

Aubrey applied the same empirical method throughout his Natural History to both natural and supernatural phenomena. He assembled evidence with care, tested it if he could and resisted easy conclusions. It’s an approach worth remembering this Halloween when fantastical tales hit your social media feed. A phantom may prove to be a load of poo.

articles.title: Anthropic’s S-1 filing spotlights safety fears and science ambitions ahead of IPO

paras.en: As artificial intelligence pioneer Anthropic prepares to go public, the company has warned users—including scientists—on Monday that advanced models may be delayed because of cybersecurity and safety threats that risk eclipsing the models’ benefits.

In documents filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission ahead of Anthropic’s expected initial public offering, the AI lab vowed to weigh the effects of its models on the public good before issuing any new products.
“Moving quickly brings AI’s benefits sooner, but moving too quickly could outrun the world’s ability to make AI systems safe,” the company wrote.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

In the filing, Anthropic acknowledged that its future relies on outpacing its competition in developing increasingly capable and complex large language models. But it also raised the risk of its AI being used for harmful purposes, such as developing biological or chemical weapons.

“We deploy technical safeguards, including automated classifiers, specifically intended to detect and block these categories of misuse,” the company warned. “But such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented.” The comments reflect a debate among AI experts over what adequate safety testing looks like in light of repeated AI breaches and hacks.

Still, Anthropic highlighted the potential for new discoveries in biology and medical sciences as a key pathway to profitability—the company currently runs at a loss in the billions of dollars. Anthropic cited its life sciences laboratory, which recently discovered a segment of DNA that bears some resemblance to CRISPR, as an example of how it could access new markets. Even that expansion presents dangers, the company acknowledged, because more traditional science and research is outside its current area of expertise.
