Anthropic also warned investors that the company will like make investments into compute power that could appear “irresponsibly large at first glance.” Those vast sums of money are part of a bet that AI will have “wild exponential” growth.
“In order to fully capture the opportunity in front of us, we need to invest more aggressively than would a business that operates in a more slowly changing technological regime,” the company wrote.

articles.title: This ‘living drug’ could change the course of autoimmune disease
articles.author: Meghan Rosen

paras.en: Two months before the treatment that would change Lynn Montgomery-Haga’s life, she could barely walk down a hallway.

In a test at the University of Colorado Anschutz, Montgomery-Haga struggled to walk 25 feet, often reaching out to the walls for support. Usually, the 49-year-old relied on her walker or wheelchair. “She had a very stiff, hesitant gait,” says Montgomery-Haga’s neurologist, Amanda Piquet.

For about a decade, Montgomery-Haga had lived with a debilitating autoimmune disease known as stiff person syndrome. The progressive condition can lock up the body’s muscles without warning, leading to falls, broken bones, excruciating pain and difficulty moving. Singer Celine Dion, who returned to the stage in September after years of battling the disease, has said it can feel “like somebody’s strangling you.”

Montgomery-Haga’s own days were marked by dizziness, fatigue and pain. And sudden muscle spasms would send her sprawling. It was like the fainting goat videos popular on the internet, she says. “They get surprised and they fall over, and there’s nothing they can do about it.”

But stiff person syndrome is no joke. It stripped Montgomery-Haga of her accounting job and her ability to drive. She couldn’t sit up in bed unless she had a safety bar to pull on. If she dropped the soap in the shower, it’d take her 10 minutes to pick it up.

Now, Montgomery-Haga hopes those struggles are finally coming to an end. That’s because a clinical trial with an experimental therapy has helped restore mobility for her — and others like her. She can stride through her living room again. She can landscape her front yard. She doesn’t have to brace herself when her dogs jump on her. And she hasn’t fallen once since the treatment. The change has been drastic, she says. “I’m just really excited about the future.”

The treatment, a type of CAR T cell therapy, extracts immune cells from a person’s body and engineers them to attack the very cells causing the disease. First used to fight cancer, CAR T is now also targeting a variety of autoimmune diseases. If given the green light by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Montgomery-Haga’s treatment would be the first such therapy approved for an autoimmune condition — and it would be the first approved treatment for stiff person syndrome.

Stiff person syndrome may be just the beginning, says Carl June, the University of Pennsylvania immunologist and oncologist who spearheaded CAR T cell therapy for cancer decades ago. The “living drug” could herald a new era of therapeutics for autoimmune diseases like lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and even multiple sclerosis. “It’s revolutionary to think how far things have gone,” June says.

But he warns that it’s far too early to know if scientists have definitively cured stiff person syndrome. And there haven’t been enough people treated to get a good handle on all the possible side effects. “There could be long-term complications in autoimmune patients that don’t happen in our cancer patients,” he says. Other researchers urge caution. “It’s very important not to oversell it,” says Marc Scherlinger, a rheumatologist at Strasbourg University Hospital in France.

For Piquet, one crucial question is how long the treatment will last. In Montgomery-Haga’s case, the answer seems to be at least two years. Montgomery-Haga still considers herself disabled, or “disabled-ish,” as she calls it. But when rating how she used to feel on a scale of one to 10, she’d put herself at a zero before treatment, she says. These days, she’s more like a seven.
What’s more, Montgomery-Haga says, “I think I’m still improving.”

There’s no single symptom that clued Montgomery-Haga in to her disease. In 2014, she started having difficulty picking things up off the floor. Then her boss asked her why she was limping — Montgomery-Haga hadn’t noticed. Her balance was off and her head felt weird, like “I was walking around in a fishbowl,” she says. It got to the point where Montgomery-Haga had difficulty crossing thresholds between rooms.

Montgomery-Haga would startle easily, prompting her body to stiffen up like a board. One time when cooking, she burned her finger, spasmed and collapsed, cracking the back of her head on the cabinets. She lay on the floor crying, but finally managed to right herself. “As soon as you hit the floor,” she says, “your muscles are like, ‘Fine,’ and you can get up again.”

Those unpredictable symptoms capture a slice of what life is like with stiff person syndrome, or SPS. The disease, which affects roughly 2 in 100,000 people in the United States, typically develops in a person’s 30s or 40s. It is about twice as common in women as in men.

Scientists don’t know what sets off the disease. But they think a person’s own antibodies start attacking a neurological network that helps muscles throughout the body relax. And when those tensed muscles are in opposition, like the biceps and triceps, they start fighting one another, Piquet says. That’s when people can end up in a stuck position, leading to stiffness. But because everyone’s immune system is different, patients’ experiences with the disease can vary greatly.

For Tara Zier, a former dentist based in Maryland, SPS started with extreme neck pain, blood pressure spikes, shortness of breath and feelings of impending doom. While some people struggle with mobility, Zier’s difficulties include standing and extreme fatigue. When she holds herself upright, her muscles clamp down on her spine like it’s in a vise. “Have you ever had a charley horse in your calf?” she asks. “Imagine one in your whole body that stops you in your tracks.”

Zier and Montgomery-Haga went years before learning what was behind their symptoms. Their cases mystified doctors — Zier saw 13 specialists and visited the emergency room nine times before getting a diagnosis. When she finally found out she had SPS three years after her first symptoms, Zier says she felt validated, like medicine was confirming what she already knew: “Something’s wrong with me.”

Montgomery-Haga’s 2018 diagnosis put her “over the moon,” she says. For nearly four years, she had gotten sicker and sicker — but doctors couldn’t tell her why. She felt as if they were giving up on her. With the diagnosis, Montgomery-Haga not only learned that SPS existed, she says, “I was told it’s treatable.”

Current treatments include muscle relaxers, anti-seizure medications and Botox injections in body parts that feel especially stiff. Although these off-label therapies can address people’s symptoms, they’re “doing nothing to treat the underlying autoimmune disease,” Piquet says. And some can come with potent side effects, like mental fog.

Zier, who has tried multiple combinations of different meds, remembers frequently losing her train of thought. She has since tapered off all but one drug, a low dose of Valium. “The trade-off,” she says, “is pain.”

People with SPS can also receive intravenous infusions of healthy antibodies, a treatment called IVIG, to decrease muscle spasms and stiffness. Montgomery-Haga found it helpful but time-consuming. She’d go to the clinic every three weeks for an infusion, which could take up to six hours.

“The bottom line is there are no FDA-approved therapies for this disease,” Piquet says. Now, the one most likely to cross the finish line first is something no one would have expected even a few years ago, CAR T pioneer June says. If you told doctors that CAR T cell therapy was going to be FDA approved for an autoimmune disease, he says, “people would have laughed.”

June may be best known for his work in cancer, but he’s been keenly following the progress in auto-immune therapy. His daughter, now in her 30s, was diagnosed with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis when she was 9 years old. For her, that’s meant over 20 years of treatment with drugs that bring a bundle of side effects, such as fatigue and risk of infections. “It would be much better to be cured,” he says.

In autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and SPS, a person’s own antibodies attack tissues throughout the body, from blood vessels to cartilage to neurons. Wiping out these rogue antibodies can stop the attacks. But CAR T cell therapy doesn’t act on the antibodies themselves. It goes straight to the source, snuffing out the cellular factories that manufacture them.

Those antibody factories are known as B cells. To eliminate them, doctors recruit T cells, which act as the body’s security system and work together to hunt down and destroy problematic cells. In the lab, scientists fine-tune these hunters, outfitting them with a molecular homing device called a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. When infused back into patients’ bodies, the newly-engineered T cells can target the antibody factories directly — like a saboteur told exactly what to destroy.

The CAR T cell therapy Lynn Montgomery-Haga received wipes out B cells, including the ones likely driving her disease. Doctors hope this therapy “resets” her immune system, getting rid of harmful B cells and letting healthy new ones take their place.

“The secret behind CAR T cell therapy is that you completely deplete B cells in the body,” says Georg Schett, a rheumatologist at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg in Germany. Temporarily wiping out a person’s B cells lets the body replace them with fresh, unproblematic ones, Schett says. He calls it an “immune reset.”

CAR T cell therapy got its start in the 2010s, when researchers used engineered T cells to target cancer. In 2017, the FDA approved the first CAR T cell therapies for two blood cancers, acute lymphoblastic leukemia and large B cell lymphoma. Soon after, scientists saw the first tantalizing hints that it might work for autoimmune diseases, too. In some cases, cancer patients with autoimmune disorders reported improvements in both conditions after treatment.
But most researchers didn’t think it could be that easy, Schett says. After all, autoimmune diseases were driven by a complex network of cell types. How could targeting just one of them work?

That thinking underwent a paradigm shift in 2021 when Schett and his team published the first major paper reporting a successful treatment with the therapy. The patient was a 20-year-old woman with a severe case of lupus, a complex, sometimes-fatal illness that can damage the kidneys and other organs. Within five weeks of CAR T cell therapy treatment, signs of her disease began to vanish.

Results like these were “unheard of,” says rheumatologist Maximilian Konig of Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore. Lupus is extremely difficult to treat, and for decades, most drugs tested against it failed. No one had ever seen the kind of improvements that Schett’s patient experienced.
After the paper came out, “everybody was talking about it,” Konig says. Today, more than five years later, the woman’s lupus hasn’t returned, Schett says. “We consider this patient cured,” he says.
The woman’s response was no fluke. The following year, Schett’s team reported similar results in five more lupus patients. All went into remission after CAR T cell therapy.
This was the true tipping point, June says. “It’s rare, very rare, that you get such striking results.”

What followed was an explosion of research around the world. Scientists are now testing CAR T cell therapy in nearly a dozen autoimmune diseases linked to harmful B cells, including lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and a connective-tissue disease known as systemic sclerosis.

Kyverna, the California-based company behind the SPS trial, is also running trials for neurological autoimmune conditions including generalized myasthenia gravis and progressive multiple sclerosis, or MS.

One reason using CAR T cell therapy for neurological conditions excites researchers is because of the cells’ potential to slip past the blood-brain barrier. That means they might be able to access pockets of smoldering inflammation inaccessible to other drugs, says neurologist Rebecca Farber of Columbia University.

That could be a huge help in diseases like MS, in which a person’s antibodies attack the protective sheaths around nerve cells, causing numbness, brain fog and difficulty walking. Still, Farber doubts that CAR T cell therapy could fix existing damage. “We’re not expecting it to repair the nervous system,” she says. But it’s possible the treatment could freeze the disease’s progress. Patients are already asking her team about future treatments.

For Piquet, who cares for roughly 100 people with SPS, Kyverna’s trial offered a compelling opportunity to help her patients. Montgomery-Haga cried when Piquet told her about the trial at one of their regular Zoom appointments. She recalls wondering, is this the treatment that “might help me be normal again?”
The good, the bad and the potentially ugly

Though Montgomery-Haga leapt at the chance to try Kyverna’s treatment, called miv-cel, CAR T cell therapy is no walk in the park. Before starting, doctors sit patients down to “talk about the good, the bad and the potentially ugly,” Piquet says.

That includes the rigorous prep work needed before people receive their engineered T cells. Patients must first get low-dose chemotherapy, which flushes T cells from the body and makes space for the new ones. Chemo can ambush the body with symptoms including hair thinning, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.

Treatment itself also carries risks. It destroys most B cells in the body — not just the ones that cause disease. That can lead to fever, inflammation and potentially risky infections. In Kyverna’s trial, for example, 15 percent of participants had severely low white blood cell counts after treatment. Such symptoms were expected, Piquet says, and were easily treated.

Other CAR T treatments seem to have fared far worse. In August, the pharmaceutical company Novartis paused clinical trials of its therapy, rap-cel, across a spectrum of autoimmune diseases after three patients died. Bristol Myers Squibb has also paused similar studies after some patients experienced neurological complications, according to the Wall Street Journal. Details of the incidents were slow to emerge and have set the field on edge. “It’s a tragedy,” Konig says. He calls such outcomes an important wake-up call.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But red flags in one trial don’t mean all CAR T products are dangerous, Konig says. That’s because many different designs and manufacturing processes exist, and scientists can’t always predict what will make one product toxic and another safe. Kyverna’s miv-cel, for instance, has been consistently well-tolerated in the more than 100 patients treated, a spokesperson for the company says.
CAR T cell therapies are transformative, Konig says. “They’re going to change the field — but there are risks.”

Another risk is that the once-vanquished disease will return. Doctors don’t know all the genetic and environmental conditions that trigger autoimmune disease. Some researchers wonder whether vulnerable individuals remain vulnerable, even after treatment. But because it often takes multiple insults for someone to tip into a state of disease, Scherlinger says, CAR T cell therapy could buy patients lots of time.

After 10 days in the hospital for her treatment, Montgomery-Haga returned to recover at home. In the following months, she started to notice some changes. It was easier getting around the house, for one. And she felt her balance and stability improving. She can now kneel down to garden and clean without the days of recovery it used to require. “I can vacuum my house,” she says. “It seems so little, but now I can vacuum!”
Montgomery-Haga can even sit down “crisscross applesauce,” she says. “I couldn’t do that for, like, 10 years.”

Four months after the treatment, Piquet’s team tested Montgomery-Haga’s walking ability. In a hallway at University of Colorado Anschutz’s research building, the team marked out 25 feet with little orange cones. At one end stood Montgomery-Haga. At the other, Piquet watched behind a video camera. This time, Montgomery-Haga’s gait was smooth and her arms were down, not hovering out into the air to catch herself if she fell. “You could see that she was walking with a lot more confidence,” Piquet says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The team saw similar results in other SPS patients. Some who had difficulty walking before treatment now wanted to run, Piquet says. “It’s incredible to just see those patients speeding down the hallway.” She remembers smiles, high fives and a sense of celebration in the air. Eight of 12 people who had used a walking aid for the initial test didn’t need one for the follow-up, Piquet reported at the American Academy of Neurology meeting in April.

In September, Kyverna reported the trial’s one-year results: Patients maintained mobility improvements, with a third completing their 25-foot walk about as fast as a healthy adult. Additionally, nearly all patients no longer rely on immuno-suppressive drugs to tamp down harmful immune activity. That’s good news because such drugs can bring all sorts of nasty side effects, like vomiting, bleeding and infections.
The results with SPS are “really something to celebrate,” June says. But only time and many more treatments will reveal how safe CAR T really is, he says.

That’s a concern for Zier, who says she wouldn’t feel comfortable trying the therapy at this point. Zier doesn’t know how she’d respond. She’s a single mother with two kids; even a rare side effect could disrupt her life in a way she may not be able to manage. And these days, she’s managing as well as she can. Zier is the founder and CEO of The Stiff Person Syndrome Research Foundation, which supports research for SPS treatments.

Kyverna is in the process of submitting miv-cel for FDA approval. The company is seeking priority review and hopes the treatment might be available to patients in 2027. If SPS is the first autoimmune disease to have an FDA-approved CAR T cell therapy, myasthenia gravis could be the second, says Warner Biddle, Kyverna’s CEO. What’s more, miv-cel also appeared to improve symptoms in six patients with severe cases of rheumatoid arthritis, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.

As for what’s next, the door is wide open. Some scientists are working to make off-the-shelf forms of CAR T that wouldn’t require personalized engineering. Others are trying to reprogram T cells directly inside people’s bodies, rather than in the lab. Still others are trying to make T cells that target only the B cells responsible for disease. In the future, doctors might use such drugs to help patients avoid the cumbersome treatment process that Montgomery-Haga endured.

Montgomery-Haga’s own future looks far different than what she had imagined a few years ago. In 2026, she took a trip to Washington, D.C., to see the monuments. Now she’d like to visit Paris, Scotland and Ireland, too.
For so many years, Montgomery-Haga has looked at trips and activities — and even household chores — that most people take for granted, thinking, “Man, I wish I could do that,” she says. “Now I can.”

articles.title: Was van Gogh’s ‘The Starry Night’ a flight of fancy or a real sky?
articles.author: Lisa Grossman

paras.en: Vincent van Gogh’s “The Starry Night” may have been based on one specific night sky: July 22, 1889, just before dawn over France.
If that’s true, it means the famous painting was based on real observations, not just van Gogh’s imagination, astronomer Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim and colleagues report October 22 in Scientific Reports.

“How could an invented sky fit the sky of a particular date this closely?” the team writes. “Observation and imagination have commonly been treated as an either/or, yet ‘The Starry Night’ shows the two coexisting on one canvas.”
Art historians typically date “The Starry Night” to mid-June 1889, based on one of van Gogh’s letters to his brother Theo.

“At last I have a landscape with olive trees, and also a new study of a starry sky,” van Gogh wrote on or about June 18. About a month earlier, van Gogh had entered a hospital in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France. “The Starry Night” is thought to represent the view through the window of his room. A short time later, van Gogh experienced an illness during which he didn’t paint for about six weeks, so most historians think “The Starry Night” must have been painted before then.

That letter is taken as strong evidence, says astronomer Donald Olson of Texas State University in San Marcos, who has written about how astronomy shows up in art history. Historians favor the June date because “van Gogh himself said so,” he says.

That assumption has led to some confusion, though. In the 1980s, two astronomers tried to match the painting’s stars to real skies in Saint-Rémy in mid-June. One proposed that the sky was from June 19, 1889, and the collection of swirly stars is the constellation Aries.

But the other concluded it couldn’t have been painted on June 19, based on cloudy weather reports in Aix-en-Provence, France, about 70 kilometers away. That study claimed the painting was “a celestial composite, constructed to make an image of the morning sky.”

Kim, who founded a telescope-building company called SLLAB Inc. in Seoul, South Korea, didn’t know about the June date when he became interested in “The Starry Night.” “Unlike previous astronomical studies, we could start freely,” he says.

Given his job, Kim had an intuition for which stars would be visible when. “People like me, who guide a telescope through its first alignment with the sky, naturally memorize where the stars are,” he says.
He was skeptical of the Aries theory. The stars in that constellation are faint enough that they wouldn’t be all that visible in the predawn sky, “hardly enough to inspire a painter,” he says.

Instead, Kim saw the stars as the Hyades star cluster, which forms a sideways V shape in the constellation Taurus. To test that theory, he and his colleagues applied a statistical technique called Procrustes shape analysis to put a number to how well the stars in the painting matched any particular constellation.

Researchers compared the V-shaped collection of stars in “The Starry Night” (first image) with those in the Hyades star cluster (middle image). The resulting graph (last image) maps the real stars (blue) and the painting’s stars (orange) against each other. They don’t overlap perfectly, but they’re suspiciously close, researchers say. The label Sn stands for “The Starry Night.” while the constellation’s Greek letters represent typical astronomy notation.

The team tested the method on another van Gogh skyscape, “Starry Night Over the Rhône,” which clearly depicts the Big Dipper. “Apart from the Big Dipper, there is no star pattern we can say for certain that Vincent painted,” Kim says. The degree of matching between the art and the sky for both paintings turned out to be similar, a major clue.

Kim also used the position and phase of the moon (a waxing gibbous on June 19, in contrast to the sharp waning crescent in the painting) and Venus to further constrain the painting’s date. He used computer simulations that weren’t available in the ‘80s to calculate the positions of celestial objects on certain dates in 1889 down to the second. He even traveled to France in June and July 2019 to try to find the field of view van Gogh would have seen from his window. Ultimately, July 22, 1889, was the best fit for the team’s data.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “I still cannot forget the moment we finally found the spot, overlaid the drawing on the view and saw it fit perfectly,” Kim says. “I was standing where Vincent had stood 130 years earlier. And the thrill I felt when I confirmed that the moon, the Hyades and Venus of July 22, 1889, fit exactly within the drawing’s field of view is still with me.”
Not to douse Kim’s enthusiasm, but that field of view may not be exactly what van Gogh saw, Olson says.

“The authors’ assumed narrow field of view, essential for their theory that the stars of the Hyades fill most of the canvas, is inconsistent with the much wider field of view required to encompass ‘The Starry Night’s’ round hills and cliffs,” he says. That casts doubt on the paper’s conclusions.

Olson proposes an experiment: Tell an amateur astronomer that “The Starry Night” depicts the Hyades and ask them to point out the star Aldebaran, which is at the bottom left of the V. In real life, this is the brightest star in the Hyades. But the painting has other much more prominent stars.

“If [the authors’] theory is correct, then this should be easy,” Olson says. Kim and colleagues identify Aldebaran as one of the two stars to the left of the cypress tree in “The Starry Night.” But Olson thinks others will see it differently. “A decent guess is that an experienced amateur astronomer, even when prompted to see the Hyades, will not identify Aldebaran as either of the two stars to the left of the cypress tree.”

articles.title: A nanoparticle revealed the tiny impact of a single gas atom
articles.author: Emily Conover

paras.en: The force exerted by a gas is usually the result of many atoms or molecules bouncing around all at once: Think of the air inside a balloon keeping it inflated. But even an individual atom can exert a tiny force. To detect that force, researchers used a laser to levitate a glass sphere, just 100 nanometers across and weighing about a quadrillionth of a gram, inside a vacuum chamber. Then, the researchers added small amounts of a heavy gas, either krypton, xenon or sulfur hexafluoride. The first two are gases made up of atoms, while the third consists of molecules.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The nanosphere was about 10 million times as massive as an individual gas particle, making the impact extremely difficult to detect. But, by monitoring the laser light that reflected from the sphere, the researchers could measure its tiny movements when hit by a gas particle. The resulting impulses were as small as a billionth of a Newton acting for one ten-trillionth of a second. And the rate of the collisions grew as the researchers introduced more gas into the chamber, increasing the pressure within.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That suggests a possible application for the technique. “This could enable a very good way to sense pressure,” says physicist Yu-Han Tseng of Yale University, especially at very low pressures — such as in space or in vacuum chambers. The system could also distinguish between the different types of gases Tseng and colleagues studied, as each one interacted differently with the nanoparticle.

A device like this could help reveal the composition of particles in space, and even on other worlds, Tseng says. “You can imagine putting it on another planet and [using] that to study the environment there.”

articles.title: Success! IBM Hits 99% Accuracy Transferring Quantum Information Between Chips
articles.author: David Nield

paras.en: Prototype quantum computers already exist, but if we're to truly realize their full potential, they need to be significantly scaled up and stabilized – and a team of researchers from IBM just announced an important step toward this goal.

The upgrade concerns the long-distance couplers (L-couplers) that connect qubits together. Qubits sit at the heart of quantum computers, and unlike the conventional bits that underpin classical computing, they're not restricted to a binary state of 1 or 0.
Scaling up quantum computers by linking multiple chips with L-couplers makes more practical sense than trying to pack ever more qubits together on the same microchip.
But the connectors need to be capable of carrying fragile quantum information over very long distances in quantum terms – 80 centimeters (31.5 inches) long in this case.
Here, the researchers linked two 120-qubit chips together with four L-couplers made of superconducting aluminum, achieving an average transfer accuracy of 99 percent, and peaking at 99.29 percent.
It's an important test for this kind of multi-channel setup, with large quantum chips currently able to transfer data through several routes.
"In the coming years quantum computers will scale up markedly in both processor complexity and module count," write the researchers in their paper.

"Such machines will need many nominally identical connections between modules. We demonstrate a practical route to realizing multiple L-couplers between large-qubit processors after the modules are mounted in a cryostat."

If classical bits can be like the heads or tails of a coin (1 or 0), then qubits can be heads, tails, or still spinning between the two until they're measured, which brings an exponential increase in computing power.
What the L-couplers are transmitting here are the quantum states of the qubits, or their spinning properties.

The team also observed that their cables lost very little energy in use, stayed operational through three cycles of warming up and cooling down, and could also transmit entanglement between the two chips.

"To our knowledge this is the first demonstration of a multi-channel quantum interconnect between large-qubit superconducting processors, and it establishes the combined L-coupler technology presented here as a viable building block for scaling modular systems," write the researchers.

IBM is going all in on the modular approach to quantum computing. The qubits and L-couplers demonstrated here are intended to be installed inside fridge-like cryogenic systems that the company unveiled back in August.
These units can keep qubits at the ultra-cold temperatures needed for quantum computing, and now we have a much better idea of how their internal electronic plumbing will work in practice.

The ultimate aim is to link hundreds of quantum chips together in these cryogenic units – cooled down to temperatures 180 times colder than deep space – and from there to deliver the world's first fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029.

"The successful connection and operation of these cryogenic modules signals a leap forward in that direction and will accelerate our progress alongside continued innovation in quantum hardware, software, and algorithms," says Jay Gambetta, director of IBM Research, who wasn't directly involved in the study.

It's a step in the right direction for these quantum computing systems, though there's still lots of work to do. The researchers noticed magnetic interference that affected signal quality; for example, and further efficiency improvements will be required before these L-couplers are actually ready to be used.

There are a dizzying number of factors to consider when it comes to developing quantum computing, from information transfer and error correction, to calculation speed and hardware practicalities, but every step like this one moves us closer to next-generation computing performance.
"These four high-fidelity L-couplers establish a practical path to scalable quantum interconnects for modular quantum computing," write the researchers.
The research has yet to be peer-reviewed, but a preprint is available on arXiv.

articles.title: An Armored Amphibian That Lived Its Whole Life at Sea? It's a Fossil First
articles.author: Jess Cockerill

paras.en: No amphibian on Earth lives in the ocean. Their porous skin – crucial for gas and water exchange – generally can't cope with the salt.
But two fossils unearthed from a Late Triassic deposit in China suggest an ancient amphibian species not only inhabited saltwater – it made a proper return to the ocean, living its whole life at sea.
Geologist Lipin Diao and colleagues present the strange new amphibian, Gerrothorax maritimus, in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution.
The two fossils were discovered by local farmers in Guanling County, in a layer of rock about 237 million years old, right in the middle of the Guizhou Triassic Fossil Sites.

The place where these Gerrothorax were found was totally submerged by seas during the Late Triassic. In other words, they seem to have inhabited a marine ecosystem, alongside ichthyosaurs, crinoids, and turtles.

"We've been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian and it's a sort of very unusual member of the lineage," says co-author and paleontologist Ryosuke Motani, of the University of California, Davis.

Both specimens were found more than 30 km [18.6 miles] from any possible nearby islands, which means it's possible they never even left the water. That's pretty wild, given that the ability to traverse land and water is what amphibians are best known for.
Unlike any living amphibian, Gerrothorax's flat body was covered in plates of hard armor, which are well preserved in the fossil specimens.

"It is unknown if stem amphibians all had permeable skin as in [modern amphibians], but even if they did, the body armor of Gerrothorax prevented water absorption through the skin, mandating water drinking and absorption from the digestive tract unlike in most extant amphibians," Diao and team write.
The researchers did consider whether these Gerrothorax specimens could have drifted out to sea after death, but with both skeletons almost fully intact, that seems doubtful.

"It is very unlikely that the two individuals… were transported over 30 km and still retained nearly complete articulation down to the limb, whereas the limb is one of the first body parts to be lost from a tetrapod carcass in the sea," they write.
"Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom," Motani adds.
"But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived."
Further analysis of the strontium isotopes in their bones offered further evidence of their marine lifestyle.
Strontium is a trace element found all over Earth, and easily accumulates in the bones of animals.

The ratio of two strontium isotopes, 87Sr and 86Sr, varies by location on land depending on the local rock, while the ocean carries much the same value across the world. The strontium in these bones matched Triassic seawater, not the rock they were buried in.

"It is most likely that the two [Gerrothorax] individuals that gave rise to the type specimens grew up drinking the seawater, whose strontium ratios are reflected in their bones," Diao and team report.
The more complete specimen of the two fossils measures at least 73.7 cm (2.4 feet) along its preserved midline, though a handful of its tail bones are missing.
"It's probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what's different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky," says Motani.
The flat, chunky shape of its body, weak limbs, and heavy body armor would've made it difficult for Gerrothorax to move around on land, if it ever made it back there at all.
The research has been published in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

articles.title: One Dose of Experimental Antibody Kept HIV-Like Virus in Remission For 4 Years in a Monkey
articles.author: Esra Öz

paras.en: HIV can fall silent without leaving the body. Hidden inside immune cells, it can survive treatment and start multiplying again when medication stops.
So researchers have started going after the hiding places themselves, with an experimental antibody tested in infant monkeys.
Given once alongside early antiviral treatment, it helped keep simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), a relative of HIV, from returning for months after medication ended in some animals.
In one monkey, the virus remained undetectable in the blood for four years of follow-up.
A team including virologist Jesse Deere and immunologist Dennis Hartigan-O'Connor at the University of California, Davis tested an approach that does not require identifying each infected cell.
In a new study published in Nature Microbiology, they targeted a broader group of cells carrying a surface protein called C-C chemokine receptor type 5 (CCR5).
HIV and SIV can use CCR5 to enter cells. Once inside, they can insert their genetic material into the cell's DNA and persist.
Infected cells that lie dormant without producing new virus form a latent viral reservoir.

Antiretroviral drugs, which prevent HIV from multiplying, control the infection but can't clear the virus from these cells. Without viral proteins to expose them, the cells are also difficult for the immune system to recognize.

The experimental antibody binds both CCR5 and CD3, a protein complex on immune cells called T cells. This directs T cells to attack cells carrying CCR5. The targets include cells that could harbor the virus and cells it could infect later.

The importance of reducing viral reservoirs has also emerged from rare cases of lasting HIV remission after stem-cell transplants. Those transplants were performed to treat cancer. The new experiment tested whether an antibody could help reduce the reservoir.
Researchers exposed 25 newborn rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) to SIV, infecting 20. A week after infection, the animals began antiretroviral treatment.

The animals had been randomly assigned to three groups before exposure. One received the drugs alone. Another also received a single dose of the experimental CCR5/CD3 antibody. A third received a different antibody targeting a cell-surface protein called CD4.
Antibody treatment began two days after the antiviral drugs. The drugs continued for 18 weeks, then were stopped to see whether the virus returned.

In every animal given drugs alone, the virus reappeared in the blood within a week. In the CD4-targeting antibody group, six of eight animals rebounded within seven days, while one remained without detectable virus through the end of follow-up.
Some recipients of the CCR5/CD3 antibody stayed in remission for much longer.

Four showed no sign of the virus in their blood for more than three months. In two, it returned after 97 and 173 days. A third had no rebound before follow-up ended at around 29 weeks. In the longest-followed animal, that period reached four years.
This prolonged absence of detectable virus after medication ends is described as remission. It doesn't, by itself, establish that the infection has been completely cleared.
The team performed further tests in three animals with sustained remission. Two had received the CCR5/CD3 antibody; one had received the antibody targeting CD4.

First, the researchers temporarily depleted CD8 T cells, which can help control viral infections. If these cells were suppressing a surviving infection, weakening that defense might allow it to rebound. No rebound occurred.

Tests of tissue from these animals found no viral genetic material. Attempts to recover infectious virus from their lymph-node cells also failed. Together, the findings support a substantial reduction in the viral reservoir.

However, one sample from the monkey followed for four years produced a tiny signal of possible viral RNA. The researchers couldn't conclusively exclude contamination. They detected no accompanying viral DNA or return of virus in the blood.

The study was small, and treatment began soon after infection. The team chose infant monkeys partly because they can rebuild immune cells quickly. So it's not known whether the approach would work similarly in adults or in longstanding infections.

The antibody also targets uninfected immune cells. The animals generally tolerated treatment, with mild reactions resolving within hours, but researchers need to investigate any effects on defenses against other infections.

"Our study demonstrates that targeting CCR5-expressing cells using the host immune system may be a surprisingly effective route to HIV cure, at least for infants that can be treated soon after infection," the study authors conclude.
The approach has not been tested in people, so researchers still need to establish its effectiveness and safety in humans.
The research has been published in Nature Microbiology.

articles.title: Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck

paras.en: Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck

- A mysterious shipwreck off Turkeyâs coast may be the oldest ever discovered, dating back approximately 4,500 years to the age of the Egyptian pyramids. Although the wooden vessel has disappeared, its surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations. Researchers believe the ship may have crashed against rocks during a storm while transporting valuable goods such as oil, wine, or tree resin.
A shipwreck off the coast of Turkey is the oldest shipwreck in the world, our team of archaeologists believes.
There’s little left of the ship itself but based on clues from its cargo – including pottery vessels – a research team I was part of has tentatively dated the wreck to around 2700–2400 BCE.
That’s about 4,500 years ago. Prior to this discovery, the world’s oldest shipwreck was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, in Greece, thought to have been from about 4,200 years ago.

Much work remains to be done to finesse the conclusions, and a paper outlining the results is yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal. Yet the discovery could transform our understanding of ancient Mediterranean connections during the Early Bronze Age.
Here, and perhaps even earlier, lie the foundations of extensive trade routes as we know them today.
Associate Professor Hakan Öniz of Akdeniz University, Antalya, has worked along this coastline for decades excavating ancient shipwrecks.

Acting on clues from local seafarers, Öniz found a shipwreck in shallow waters off Kekova, west of Antalya in Turkey, in 2024. Earlier this year, he contacted me and asked if I would help date some of the pottery vessels found on this wreck.

As an archaeologist specializing in desert sites, this was a singular experience. New technology, water-logged methods of excavation and laborious conservation techniques were the new normal. Yet there is always room for learning new skills in life.

Of the ship itself there is now nothing to see, owing to underwater exposure. Yet the research team has now estimated the ship and its cargo dates to around 2700–2400 BCE. However, the precise dating is still under consideration. Earlier or later dates on either side of this initial determination are also possible.
This discovery promises to re-write our understanding of early trade networks from around 4,500 years ago.
The ship is a “missing piece” in the story of networks, trade and commodity exchange in the wider eastern Mediterranean. This era includes the pyramid age of Giza and its mighty pharaohs.
What remains under the sea is a time capsule of ancient trade.
Although its direction was not known, the boat was evidently traveling along the coast of southern Turkey.

Now resting on the seabed between two islands, it is apparent the ship likely sought refuge in the lee waters during a storm. One could imagine the terror of the sailors – possibly coastal people from the Levant region – as their ship crashed against the rocks.
While timbers from the ship disappeared long ago, the remains of its precious cargo were embedded in the rocky slope along the Kekova coast.
Divers worked over the past four months to extract its pottery from barnacles clinging to the rocky underwater slope.
Pottery is like plastic: it never goes away and just breaks down into smaller and smaller pieces.
Yet humble pottery vessels hold many clues about the past.
In this case, the cargo included large ceramic storage vessels or amphorae which once contained products from regions of the eastern Mediterranean.
The pots were large ovoid, flat-based jars with two handles, many featuring a raised horizontal clay “belt” around the widest part of the jar.
Through these vessels was possible to ascertain many pieces of information. This includes the likely origin of the jars and the contents exchanged across the region.
Importantly, the shape and manufacturing technique of the pots themselves help us date the cargo. By extension, this includes also the date of other pottery, and the ship itself.
Compared to later periods, trade and exchange in the eastern Mediterranean during the third millennium (3000–2000 BCE) is poorly understood.
Maritime voyages during the that period are known from Egyptian texts, pottery vessels and raw materials from ancient tombs.
Around the same time as this ship struck the rocks, the ancient Egyptians were trading in the eastern Mediterranean through the port of Byblos in Lebanon.
Commodities such as cedar, tin/lead, oils, tree resins, lapis lazuli and silver, all materials that Egypt lacked, were imported by the Egyptian state.
Recent scientific research also reveals that silver was acquired by the Egyptian state around 2600 BCE. Analyses showed this silver was acquired from the Lavrion mines east of modern Athens.
While it is unlikely Egyptian ships made this journey, boats like the Kekova ship may have used the route as part of an extended international maritime network.

And what was in the jars? Remarkably there were still residues visible to the naked eye. Again, scientific analyses are pending, but could be some of the products mentioned in the Egyptian texts, possibly olive oil, wine or tree resin.

The ship may have acquired its pottery from several ports on their journey. Our best assessment at this stage of research is that some of the “belted” jars (or clays used to make them) may have originated in the Central Jordan Valley.

The coast of southern Turkey is littered with ancient shipwrecks. While maritime archaeology is a relatively recent phenomenon, some of the world’s most famous wrecks have been discovered there. Who knows what other secrets these waters hold.

The research on which this article is based was led by Associate Professor Hakan Öniz, head of the Division of Mediterranean Underwater Cultural Heritage Research, and the Department of Restoration and Conservation of Cultural Heritage in the Faculty of Art at the Akdeniz University, Antalya, Turkey.

Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Karin Sowada, Senior Lecturer in Archaeology and Director of the Australian Centre for Egyptology, Macquarie University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

paras.en: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
- Norwegian University of Science and Technology

- Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).
Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.
Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.
One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.
"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.
Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.
The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.
Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.
Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.
A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.
By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.
"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

articles.title: New 3D thermal invisibility cloak makes objects disappear from infrared cameras

paras.en: New 3D thermal invisibility cloak makes objects disappear from infrared cameras
- University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, News Bureau

- Researchers have developed a groundbreaking 3D invisibility cloak that can hide complex objects from infrared cameras while protecting them from extreme heat and cold. Instead of blocking heat, the device guides it around an object, making the object appear invisible to thermal imaging from virtually any direction. Successfully built and tested, the cloak could transform electronics cooling, thermal protection, and stealth technology.

Scientists have developed and tested the first three-dimensional thermal invisibility cloak, a device that can conceal objects from infrared cameras while protecting them from extreme temperatures. The breakthrough could lead to new ways to cool microchips, safeguard delicate electronics, and prevent equipment from being detected through its thermal signature.

The cloak can conceal objects with a wide variety of shapes, regardless of the direction from which heat approaches. Earlier thermal cloaks were limited to two dimensions or worked only when heat traveled in a particular direction. The new design overcomes these restrictions by directing heat around a hidden object rather than simply blocking it. As a result, infrared imaging shows a temperature pattern that makes the object appear to be absent.

The research was conducted by University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign civil and environmental engineering professor Shelly Zhang, postdoctoral researcher Weichen Li, and graduate student Yibo Wang, in collaboration with professor Ole Sigmund of the Technical University of Denmark. Their findings were published in Nature Communications.

"A real thermal cloak should work no matter where the heat comes from," Zhang said. "Our device can hide a complex 3D object in an infinite number of directions while keeping the temperature inside stable and protected."
A New Material Makes 3D Thermal Invisibility Possible

Creating a thermal cloak that functions in three dimensions has been a longstanding challenge. Previous experimental devices could redirect heat only across a flat surface or along one direction of heat flow, leaving them far short of the capabilities needed for a fully three-dimensional cloak.

To overcome these limitations, the researchers revisited the foundational principles of transformation thermotics, a field that explores how heat can be redirected through specially designed materials. They focused on a central question: "What kind of material structure could cover almost all the thermal properties needed for a perfect cloak?"

The solution was a new lattice-based material whose structure can be independently adjusted along three directions. These changes allow the researchers to control how efficiently heat passes through different parts of the cloak. Compared with previous designs, the material can achieve a much broader range of thermal conductivities, closely approaching the properties predicted to be necessary for ideal thermal cloaking.

Importantly, the researchers went beyond computer simulations and constructed a working device. They used 3D metal printing to produce an intricate aluminum lattice, which provides pathways for efficient heat conduction. They then used mold casting to fill the remaining spaces with a rubber-like material that conducts heat poorly. Together, these materials create a structure that can carefully control the movement of heat.
Infrared Camera Tests Confirm the Cloak Works

To evaluate the device, the team positioned it between hot and cold regions, establishing a temperature difference that caused heat to flow through the surrounding environment. They monitored the resulting temperature patterns with an infrared camera to determine whether the cloak could successfully redirect heat around the concealed area.

The experiments showed that the device could guide heat around the hidden region while preserving the surrounding temperature pattern. To an infrared camera, the area appeared much as it would if no object were present. At the same time, temperatures inside the cloak remained uniform, shielding the concealed space from the extreme conditions outside.

The researchers also tested whether the cloak could accommodate unusually complicated objects. They successfully concealed intricate three-dimensional geometries, including detailed shapes resembling human heads. According to the team, earlier experimental thermal cloaks have not demonstrated a comparable combination of geometric complexity and cloaking performance.
Potential Applications in Electronics and Stealth Technology

The ability to control heat in three dimensions could have important implications across several industries. In electronics, the technology could help engineers direct heat away from sensitive components, improve thermal management in microchips, and protect devices operating under demanding conditions.

The researchers also see potential applications in security and defense. Future versions of the technology might help conceal people or equipment from thermal detection systems or shield valuable assets from severe temperature conditions. These uses would build on the device's demonstrated ability to redirect external heat while keeping the protected region thermally stable.

"Any field that needs precise control of heat or needs to protect something from being detected thermally could benefit from this work," Zhang said. "But we also see it more broadly: it's about hiding and protecting information that is carried by heat."
The Next Challenge Is Hiding Objects That Generate Heat

Although the current cloak represents a major advance, the researchers want to develop more sophisticated versions capable of performing additional functions. One particularly important goal is to conceal objects that produce heat themselves, rather than only protecting them from heat originating outside the cloak.

Achieving this would require materials that can actively control heat within the concealed region. Instead of simply redirecting incoming heat, a future cloak would need to concentrate, distribute, or guide thermal energy as conditions change. Such capabilities could expand the technology's usefulness in electronics, thermal protection, and applications involving infrared detection.

"We've shown that a true 3D omnidirectional thermal cloak is possible," Zhang said. "The next step is to make cloaks that don't just hide and protect, but also actively manipulate heat in useful ways."

The research received support from the National Science Foundation, the Villum Foundation, and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. Zhang is also affiliated with mechanical science and engineering and the National Center for Supercomputing Applications at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 26, 2004: Cassini spacecraft takes 1st-ever closeup photos of Saturn moon Titan
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

paras.en: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan.

The Cassini spacecraft would later drop off a probe on Titan named Huygens, which was a European spacecraft that hitched a ride to the Saturn system with the Cassini mission. But before Cassini dropped off its robotic passenger, it flew by Titan a few times and took some amazing photos.

Cassini completed its first flyby on July 3, 2004, but when it swung by a second time on Oct. 26, it got about 300 times closer than it did the first time. At the closest point of this flyby, Cassini was 745 miles (1,200 kilometers) away from the surface of Titan. The spacecraft took hundreds of photos during this flyby, and these were the highest resolution views of Titan anyone had ever seen.

Astronomers knew Saturn's moon Titan had an atmosphere before Cassini arrived at the smog-shrouded moon, but the spacecraft's first photos (and innumerable more that followed) revealed a strange world that looked eerily similar to what scientists suspect a young Earth might have been like.

The first close-up views of Titan by Cassini showed a large continent-sized region that scienitsts called Xanadu. It included bright features that hinted at a mountain range, as well as a large basin and smooth plains regions.

In all, Cassini would make 127 close flybys of Titan during its 13 years at Saturn before the mission ended in 2017. The probe even dropped the European Huygens lander on Titan, which landed in January 2005, to see the moon's surface first hand.

This flyby image of Titan (and other instrument observations taken at the same time) allowed scientists to measure Titan's atmosphere density and composition to better plan the path and descent for the Hygens lander.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

articles.title: Analog astronauts: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.author: Michaela Musilova

paras.en: I have been dreaming of doing research in space as an astronaut my whole life, but for some reason, the thought of working underwater made me nervous. I’ve known for a long time that astronauts train underwater to simulate different scenarios they’re likely to experience in space. Diving was never an issue for me, either — I even made it as far as becoming a certified rescue diver. So what was the problem?

This summer, I led a simulated space mission in an underwater habitat called the Jules’ Undersea Lab. It is a research station that is located 22 feet (6.7 meters) underwater near Key Largo, Florida. You have to scuba dive to get in and out of the station. To become an aquanaut, you have to stay underwater for at least 24 hours in a so-called state of saturation.

I had been preparing for many years for this aquanaut experience, both as a scientist and as an analog astronaut. An analog astronaut is someone who takes part in a simulated space mission, where they live and work in conditions similar to those that astronauts on the International Space Station (ISS) experience today, or will one day experience on the moon and Mars.

I’m no stranger to simulated space missions, either; I have been the Commander of almost 40 such missions in different facilities around the world. Almost all of those missions were on land, though, which made them substantially safer than a mission underwater. The risks of something going wrong during a simulated spacewalk or even during basic maintenance activities underwater are significantly higher than during standard analog missions on land.

Despite knowing all of that, a mission underwater was something I definitely wanted to experience to improve my skills as a leader, researcher and diver. However, the closer I got to the start of the mission, the more worried I became. My brain went through all the terrible scenarios that could occur during the mission while I was preparing for it — from someone’s gear malfunctioning during a spacewalk underwater to storms forcing us to evacuate in the middle of the night. Perhaps I still had some trauma from watching "The Abyss" by James Cameron as a child 😉.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Our mission was symbolically called SEA STAR, and I spent over a year organizing it. It took some time to get the right team and research projects together, as well as the necessary funding. My goal was to lead a mission simulating what astronauts go through on the ISS, both in terms of the diverse projects they work on and the challenges they face living in space. Only for us the deadly environment surrounding us wasn’t space, but water.

Since the health and safety of the crew is at higher risk during underwater missions, the team has to adhere to more strict procedures than they would need to during a simulated space mission on land. That, in turn, makes the mission feel more similar to an astronaut’s mission in space. The underwater environment also allowed us to perform neutral buoyancy experiments during simulated spacewalks, as well as scientific research focused on the effects of high atmospheric pressures on humans.

Our SEA STAR crew was composed of experienced analog astronauts and divers. Paul Bakken, an experimental engineer, was our Executive Officer responsible for most of the mission’s logistics. The Health and Safety Officer was Dr. Brandy Nunez, who performed microgreens research on top of overseeing the wellbeing of the crew. Our team’s Mission Specialist was Jenn Pint, who is an industrial safety expert. She was in charge of a project focused on developing a taxonomy for analyzing environmental and crew interaction factors in a space analog environment, in collaboration with Interstellar Performance Labs.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: As the Commander of the crew, my main responsibilities were to make sure the crew was safe, in good health and spirits, getting along well and on top of their work. I worked with Paul to plan the mission’s schedule and to tweak it as needed — for instance, when we faced unexpected problems or some things were taking longer than planned. I also brought several research and educational projects with me on the mission, which I performed on top of my Commander duties.

Even though I was a bit concerned about the risks of the aquanaut mission before it started, I trusted my crew. I knew that we would find a way to problem-solve and face the challenges that would come our way, just like astronauts do in space. I was also looking forward to all of the interesting experiments that we had planned for the mission, which ranged from cognitive research under pressure to testing environmental student sensors.

In the end, I mostly had to trust myself that I had what it takes to not only perform this mission, but also to lead it. As I put on my scuba gear, before diving underwater for five days, I focused on the positive aspects of the mission. The nervous voices in my head made themselves heard a couple of times while I entered the water. Nevertheless, I was completely calm by the time I took my last breath of Earth air. I just waved at our collaborators on land, submerged myself and started our intense “space,” a.k.a. underwater, mission.

Michaela has been conducting space-related research at institutions around the world, including NASA, ESA, CalTech, the Canada-France-Hawaii telescope and many others. She was the Commander of 40 simulated missions to the Moon and Mars — the most missions led to date.
